VIII. Sister Anna del Salvatore Elected Provincial of the Houses in Sicily

In a short span of time, Sister Anna del Salvatore passed successively from one House to another where her pious, intelligent, and diligent work was urgently needed; thus Genoa, Macerata, Naples, Rome, to say nothing of other cities, saw the good Daughter of St. Anne always ready for sacrifice to relieve suffering humanity. In her passing, she left behind a luminous flash of that heavenly light with which she was radiant, and an enduring memory of her inexhaustible charity.

But if great was the regard in which Sister Anna del Salvatore was publicly held, no less great was the esteem she enjoyed within the Institute of which she was a member, and at the General Chapter held at the Mother House in Piacenza, a Chapter attended by all the Superiors of the Order, she was elected by unanimous vote Provincial of all the Houses of the Daughters of St. Anne in Sicily. One can easily imagine how great the importance of this office is, considering that the one chosen must enjoy the full trust of the Superiors, whose representative she is, if not with full powers, certainly with a very broad freedom of action.

She accepted the new office, though she considered herself unworthy of it, because such was the will of her Mother and the wish of her fellow sisters, trusting in the Lord, who, just as He had helped her carry out the office of Superior, would also sustain her on the very rugged path she now had to travel. She no longer had just one House to think of, but several: she no longer had to watch over only the sisters of her own Community, but all those of the Sicilian island, and under the heavy weight of this double responsibility she would have succumbed, had her unshaken faith in divine Mercy and her iron will not to draw back before the obstacles that would hinder her from fulfilling her duty not given her the courage needed to sustain this new trial.

She set to work, and it would be an arduous task, not to say impossible, to enumerate all the wonders of her charity, were Termini Imerese, Trapani, Sciacca, Sambuca Zabut, Girgenti, Linguaglossa, Adernò, and very many other Sicilian towns, which for brevity I do not name, not in a position to testify, each for its own part, to what they witnessed and how great is their gratitude and veneration for her who knew, through the power of her winning virtues, how to make herself worthy of the love of God and the gratitude and reverence of men.

Sister Anna del Salvatore, a true angel of charity, was wherever there were sorrows to soothe, tears to dry; and in the hospitals, the asylums, the boarding schools, the houses of correction, the foundling homes entrusted to the Daughters of St. Anne, one would have seen her, solicitous, pious, patient, in the sublime exercise of her duties as Provincial, counseling her fellow sisters with her wise and prudent judgment, helping them attentively, and encouraging them to sacrifice by her admirable example.

Blessed was she, who, after a day entirely devoted to privations and the heaviest toil for the relief of those who suffered, could linger in sweet nighttime conversations with her Jesus, her comfort and her hope, to whom she dedicated the hours of rest.

O holy soul, what did you find so refreshing in that inexhaustible fount of Goodness, Wisdom, and Love? Surely such paradisal satisfactions as to make you insensible to the need for rest, common to all human beings.

In the morning, after Holy Communion and Mass, she was again at work, full of energy and courage, and labored until late in the evening. But how did she provide for reinvigorating her body? Not with food, for she remained fasting until the hour of the refectory, where she took a light meal of a little bread and a little cooked or raw vegetable, as the Community's cook prepared for her, and washed down this more than meager, insufficient food with a glass of water. Nor with rest, for she never lay down to sleep; so true is this that, while she took care that every sister in every house under her direct supervision had a good bed, provided with the necessary linens, she herself was without one; and to anyone who observed that she too ought to think of resting, she would answer that she had no need to lie down in order to rest and sleep, and that a bed would therefore be, for her, a superfluous thing, a luxury, since she made no use of one. "Should I fall ill," she would conclude, "I would indeed find some compassionate fellow sister who would give up her bed to me, but meanwhile, thank God, I enjoy excellent health, and here is my best bed" — and she pointed to a chair — "it serves me marvelously!" And when the whole Community slept the peaceful sleep of one who, in work and self-sacrifice, has spent the day in holiness, what did she do? With all possible care, so as not to wake some sister and so be discovered, she would shut herself in the Chapel, and there, praying on her knees before the Blessed Sacrament, would pass the whole night, a night of ecstasy, of happiness and bliss for her, who desired nothing else than to be close to Him to whom all her aspiration and thought were directed.

One would have to have a very weak faith not to believe that only God's grace could work such a wonder. Without it, how could Sister Anna del Salvatore, a human creature, therefore also subject to human frailties, have sustained her daily toils, had she not resorted to material means, such as food, strengthening drinks, and rest, which would have served to restore her lost strength? It is clear that there is something miraculous in all this, and God worked it so that the merits of his faithful servant might shine forth all the more, merits for which a crown of immortal glory was being woven in Heaven.

Just as her special gifts had made her admired and respected by the sisters of the Houses to which she had been sent, one by one, with the office of Superior, so now they had, in her capacity as Provincial, won her such prestige that it was enough for her to speak for not only the Sisters of all the Houses of Sicily, but also the priests and lay people who had dealings with her, to feel drawn to her by deep reverence and moved to satisfy her wishes. And what could Sister Anna del Salvatore, in her complete disregard for herself, in her strict observance of the holy Vow of Poverty, in her deep love for the Institute, desire except that this redound to the good of the Institute itself? To obtain this she submitted to the most arduous undertakings, strengthened by the thought that St. Anne and her dear Mother would bless her work, which she considered a very poor thing, and would guide her on the path she had to tread, preserving her from the most terrible enemy she feared, that is, from any occasion of displeasing the Lord.

A most faithful daughter, she saw only through the eyes of her venerated Mother, just as she heard only through her ears. A single word was enough, but what am I saying? a gesture revealing her will was enough for Sister Anna del Salvatore to be ready to obey. I will say more: she made a special study of anticipating her wishes, and a "well done!" from the Mother was, for this excellent Sister, the most coveted reward. And the Mother, who knew to what degree of perfection her good daughter had risen, and how much affection she bore her, turned to her prayers whenever she needed to obtain some grace from God for the Institute's benefit. The Sister, without losing time and mistrustful of herself, would gather her fellow sisters around her and invite them, ardently and fervently, to pray with her. Those prayers were laid by the Angels at the foot of God's throne, and He received them graciously and granted the grace sought.

Nothing was denied her of all she asked of Him who was the Lord's favorite. Of the earthly she had nothing but her mortal remains; her soul was a thing wholly heavenly, and was not to remain here below much longer.

Without anyone noticing, not even herself, Sister Anna del Salvatore was moving rapidly towards the beginning of that life which would never end. Her toils, fasts, vigils, and disciplines, if they had made her soul beautiful and great, had also slowly worn away her existence. What befell the good Sister's body was what happens to a flower in whose calyx a gnawing worm insinuates itself. This, bit by bit, unnoticed, consumes its petals, which first lose their color, then wilt and fall withered to the ground. And when one day, feeling her strength spent and tormented by an inner ailment, she had to give herself up as beaten and take to her bed, every remedy was judged useless. God wanted her for Himself, and human art and science surely cannot struggle against the inscrutable decrees of Providence.

Sister Anna del Salvatore suffered a great deal, but in writing to Mother Gattorno she never made the slightest allusion to her condition; indeed, she had strictly forbidden the sisters, who sensed the impending calamity, to let her know of it, always for fear of grieving her, and in the hope that it might be a curable illness. "Let us spare the dear Mother this sorrow for now," she said, "she already has too many, poor dear!" So it was that the Mother, not knowing what was happening in the House of Palermo, telegraphed one day to the Provincial, asking her to go, on urgent Institute business, to Trapani. Who, who ever, but Sister Anna del Salvatore, in whom the virtue of obedience was raised to its highest degree, would have found the strength to fight the 104-degree fever tormenting her, to rise from her bed and give vigor to her already ruined body, in order to comply with the order received? At Trapani she carried out her mission in a single day, and returned to Palermo in so alarming a state that the sisters, frightened, put her back to bed, from which she never rose again.

IX. Agony and Death of Sister Anna del Salvatore

The illness made rapid progress; by now the silence towards the Mother was becoming, on the sisters' part, an unforgivable fault; and so, with a heart torn apart, one of them gives her the dreadful news of the imminent catastrophe.

It is easier to imagine than to describe the grief the Mother felt at this dire announcement! So a life so holy and precious would soon be extinguished! So the Institute would forever lose one of its strongest pillars, one of the most tireless workers for its welfare, and a dearly beloved daughter would be taken from her on earth! God, what anguish for that soul! And yet this was the Lord's will, and: Fiat. He who has numbered the days of every mortal has also numbered those of Sister Anna del Salvatore; she must die! The Angels await her in Heaven, and her blessed soul will soon take flight towards the eternal joy awaiting it. She has the right to it, since God ordained it as the reward for those who, modeling themselves as she did on the life of Jesus Christ, His beloved Son, will earn it. And Sister Anna del Salvatore, while everyone weeps, sensing her approaching end, raises her soul in blessed ecstasy to Heaven and smiles at the thought that soon she would enjoy that eternal, infinite, inestimable Good which had, her whole life long, been the center of her most ardent aspirations.

During her illness too, she gave proof of the virtues that adorned her soul. Patient in suffering, humble in expressing her very limited wishes, affectionate as always towards the sisters, to whom, even ill, her thoughts turned; pious, devout, resigned, she awaited eagerly the death that, freeing her from the bonds of the body, would allow her to be united forever with her beloved spouse Jesus. Even in illness there stood out, like a diamond in the dazzling and precious crown of her chosen virtues, holy Obedience, by virtue of which she bent in all things to the will of whoever cared for her, even when her own will would have resolutely opposed it. And it was out of love for holy Obedience that she submitted to taking foods other than the vegetables to which her stomach had been accustomed for years, and that she got up, staggering, one morning to receive Communion in the Chapel with her fellow sisters, and to stay at work with them the whole day, since the Mother had ordered this by telegram, by the will of God, as an extraordinary proof of the virtue of holy Obedience. And here an event occurred that surprised even the doctors. After having made Holy Communion, the sister felt better; indeed, her fever having instantly ceased, she felt cured, and for three or four days was up and about with the others. Only, when she took food, she would say: "This goes in but doesn't come out anymore." The sisters, who were used to her playful manner, laughed at this; but alas, the Provincial was not joking! A terrible illness, peritonitis, developed: it rarely forgives, and so it was that, without time to warn the Mother that the Provincial had fallen ill again, the poor woman found herself at the end of her life.

It is difficult to imagine how deeply the people of Palermo felt the approaching calamity of the loss of Sister Anna del Salvatore. There was a continual stream of people, from the wealthy lady to the humble woman, from the powerful patrician to the lowliest commoner, going to the House to ask for news of the sick woman, many with tears in their eyes, all with the deepest sadness in their hearts. Prayers, blessings, triduums, and novenas were made, within and outside the Institute, for her recovery, but in vain; she was already ripe for Heaven, to which she would soon ascend!

I omit speaking of the grief in which the Community was plunged; no words would suffice for it. They were most devoted daughters losing a mother who had always been for them an inexhaustible fount of benevolence and charity. They were sisters who saw, before their very eyes, in the flower of her age, at 40, the elder sister, who by word and by the virtue of example had taught them the path to walk to reach Paradise, fading away; and they, poor souls, were as though cast into the immensity of this calamity, which they were powerless to remedy. Consumed in furtive tears, they lavished affectionate care on the dying woman, who, with her usual smile upon her lips, pressed the hand now of one, now of another, as a token of her gratitude. She alone, in so grave a moment, showed herself calm and serene. She was reaching the end of her pilgrimage, the goal to which she had always so ardently aspired, and welcomed death as a gift from Heaven, comforted by the hope of being one day united forever, in the bosom of her Jesus, with those she was leaving on earth.

But the illness grew worse, and the hour of her departure was about to strike. She asks for and receives the last comforts of our holy Religion, and one cannot, without feeling deeply moved, describe the solemn moment in which she received the Holy Viaticum. The Priest, followed by the weeping sisters, enters the room where candles burn; the sick woman sits up on the bed with her hands joined, her mouth smiling and her eyes turned to Heaven, almost as if she could glimpse there the hierarchy of the Blessed awaiting her; and when the Sacred Host is brought to her lips, a ray of Paradise is reflected on that pale and gaunt face, transforming it into the face of a saint. Those present look on in rapture and murmur fervent prayers.

After the Holy Viaticum, the Sacrament of Extreme Unction is administered to her, which she receives no less devoutly; then, as if her task on earth were finished, she withdraws wholly into herself and prays softly, pressing frequent and warm kisses upon her Crucifix, which she holds clasped in her hands. Thus passed the day of June 7, 1885. It is eleven o'clock at night, and the poor sisters, crushed with grief, kneel around their Superior's little bed, and amid sobs beg her forgiveness for faults committed against her. The dying woman opens her eyes, sees them, listens to their words broken by moans, and, ever tender towards them, forgets her own blessedness to share in their grief. She searches for all of them with her languid gaze; she recognizes, one by one, those companions of her sacrifice, and seems to want to speak one last affectionate word to each of them. But, feeling herself unable to do so, since her strength fails her, she asks the confessor to bless them, and then, making one last effort of will, she commends them, with a voice fading away, in brief, broken phrases, always to be observant of the holy Rules and to love the Mother sincerely, and rejoices when the sisters, in unison, give her their word that they would fulfill her last wish.

But her breathing becomes labored, her tongue stiffens, and she can scarcely pronounce the names of Jesus, Joseph, Mary, and St. Anne, and stammer that of the Mother. Oh, how she would have wished to see her once more; but everyone had been so blinded by the sad event that no one had thought to telegraph the Mother that the Provincial had taken a turn for the worse again, and was, against all expectation, reduced to her last moments.

And when finally the Mother was telegraphed, she, being on the mainland, could do nothing else for her dying daughter but send her a blessing by telegram, which arrived when she had already breathed her last in the kiss of the Lord.

Oh, how peaceful and serene is the final hour of one who has lived a blameless life wholly consecrated to the service of God! Sister Anna del Salvatore is no longer on earth, where she gave the sublime spectacle of a life wholly of piety and truly Christian charity; but a time will come, which I trust is not far off, when her lofty merits will be universally recognized, and this star, which shines so brightly among all those that sparkle in the Heaven of Holy Mother Church, will be granted, even on earth, that halo of immortal glory she earned by serving God through the practice of every virtue.

X. Funeral Honors Paid to the Remains of Sister Anna del Salvatore

News of the bitter loss spread through Palermo with the speed of lightning, and the mourning was universal. Very many recalled the benefits they had received from Sister Anna del Salvatore; everyone, praising her virtues, grieved that so perfect a creature had been so soon snatched away from the earth, where, with charity and example, she could have worked wonders. And while the Mother and the Institute, plunged in the deepest grief, saw to it that the obsequies prescribed by the holy Rules were given to the deceased, and that her soul be prayed for in suffrage in every Community, Palermo prepared to give the deceased the fullest testimony of esteem and sorrow, and Their Excellencies the Prince and Princess of Fitalia ordered that, at their own expense, the deceased be photographed.

Meanwhile the newspaper "La Sicilia Cattolica" published the obituary, which I faithfully reproduce here: "On the Death of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, Provincial Superior of the Daughters of St. Anne.

A tomb opened on the evening of June 7 to receive the mortal remains of a soul dear to God, a model of the perfect religious, an honor to the deserving Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne.

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, superior of the house of the Nursing Sisters and Provincial Superior of the Daughters of St. Anne in Sicily, on the 7th of this month at 11 p.m. breathed out her lovely soul in the smile of the Angels and the embrace of God; and while the grieving sisters around the precious body gave vent in copious tears to their irreparable loss, the sorrowful news, spreading through our city, filled with grief all who had the good fortune to know and come near so rare a woman and so perfect a religious, and to appreciate her uncommon virtues. 'She was an Angel! She was a saint! She was a woman of charity! She was a model of virtue!' one hears repeated from every mouth; nor do such expressions spring from hearts biased by affection, but it is the irresistible force of truth and of virtue which imposes itself even on the most depraved consciences, and wrings confession and praise even from tongues accustomed to infamy and slander. So it happens with a soul upon which the Lord has stamped in mysterious ciphers the perceptible sign of predestination, and which He has destined to shine like a luminous star of virtue amid the darkness of a corrupt age.

And such did Sister Anna del Salvatore truly show herself to be, by which she became dear and admirable to all, just as today her departure has become painful to all.

Nor is this the place to trace the rare virtues that, like fragrant flowers, adorned the springtime of her precious life, it being known besides that from girlhood she was so devoted to the things of God, and so loving of Christian mortification, as to always show herself above her years, and anticipated by the Lord's grace. And indeed it was the Lord Himself who formed and educated that virgin heart in the exquisite sentiments of piety and the lofty meanings of the spiritual life, whereby she, matured by grace and informed by heavenly love, was later to shine forth in the holy Institute, to which she was a luster and an honor, and which today mourns her loss bitterly.

She was scarcely twenty; and already her Beloved was calling her, with a sweet and irresistible voice, to consecrate herself wholly to his love and to charity towards her neighbor in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne.

This beneficent and providential institution was barely three years old, and it seemed as though the Lord had inspired it for her. The life spent in charity and sacrifice that forms that institute's program, the desire to make fruitful and active the love she felt for her neighbor, and the heroic virtues of that lady, no less noble than pious, who with generous zeal of charity stripped herself of all she had to found the charitable institute, were such motives to the heart of our twenty-year-old young woman that she did not delay an instant in answering faithfully the voice of God, and became a daughter of St. Anne.

And oh, how true it is that religious institutes are chosen gardens, watered by God's grace and made fruitful by the eternal sun, where pious souls, like flourishing plants, thrive marvelously and strengthen themselves for still harder virtue; and it was here that the lamented Sister Anna del Salvatore, like a fruitful tree, rooted in faith, watered by a greater abundance of heavenly grace, spread out her beneficent branches, and appeared rich in precious fruits of virtue. Ah! She was such that at the mere approach to her one remained captivated as if by enchantment, not knowing which to admire first in her, her deep humility or her dignified bearing; her gentleness of manner or her sobriety in dealing with others; the strength of a lion or the meekness of a lamb; the zeal that consumes or the charity that has compassion. She was one of those beings who shine with a light clear, beautiful, consoling, yet at once mysterious and indefinable, like the very light of God; what shall be said of her charity towards the sick? Ah, "why doesn't the superior come?" the sisters were often heard to repeat; "when she comes we feel better." And indeed the mere sight of her refreshed the souls of the poor sick, and God's spirit instilled in her such depths of compassion for sufferers that she would have ground and worn herself away just to bring comfort and relief to the wretched languishing.

Her humility left one confounded, and there was never an occasion on which anyone managed, whether by words or by deeds, to wrest from her the coveted primacy of the last place. "Ah, when will I be converted? Ah, I still have not converted!" she was often heard to exclaim, so it is no wonder that she hated herself to the point of declaring merciless war on her body, on her senses, giving herself to the most laborious and austere life out of love for that God who drew and united her to Himself. Enormous toils, tireless activity, continual journeys, countless hardships wore away a life that may be said to have been consumed for God and for the benefit of her neighbor. But what were her austerities, what her prayers, what her outpourings of love for God? what her food, what her bed, how did she spend her nights, how did she occupy her days?

Who can lift this veil, save those to whom, by title of spiritual direction, it was given to know that much which might escape the resourceful and inviolable secrecy with which this woman of God was wont to cover her rare virtues?

But it is in vain that all the efforts of the deepest humility strive to keep some flash of light, amid the darkness of a hidden life, from sometimes revealing the secret working of grace, and from bringing to light virtues poorly concealed.

It is no wonder, then, that eminent persons, ladies of rank, and noble dames took pride in seeking out and drawing near to the humble Daughter of St. Anne, to ask her for comfort, to request her prayers, to seek her advice, to pour out in her charitable heart their sorrows and anguish; and let the noble and pious Princess of Fitalia stand for them all, who more than any other dealt closely with her, admired her virtues, attended her agony, and wept at her sorrowful loss.

And what wonder, when persons, through notorious impiety and systematic hatred of anything savoring of religion, felt themselves drawn to her beautiful virtues, and bowed in benevolence towards her holy Institute?

But alas! So precious a life was so soon to decline towards its sunset. Who would not have tried to hold back a little longer, on the horizon, this luminous star of virtue? But she, who had scarcely passed her eighth lustrum, was already rich in merits and ripe for heaven.

It was indeed in the last days of this past April that the fatal illness struck her, from which she would never recover. With difficulty, and once nature had been overcome by the illness, she had to take to her bed, where she lay like a little flame that quivers all about as it strives to detach itself from the earth and lose itself in the vast fields of heaven.

And it was in those final moments that she was suddenly to revive and give new displays of virtue before being extinguished.

She had been ill only three or four days when a telegram arrived from the Mother General, ordering her to go to Trapani, where a new House of the Institute had been opened. The poor sick woman trembles, but does not hesitate; she gathers the last strength remaining to her, and for Jesus Christ, for obedience, and for her beloved Institute, spends it entirely; she sets out and goes where obedience calls her, but after a few days returns in the worst state: her sacrifice was already consummated: God had already accepted it with pleasure, and hastened to call her to her crown. Oh, what examples of heroic patience, of inner calm, she gave to those fortunate enough to witness her final agonies! What sweet perfumes of virtue exhaled from that deathbed! What an air of Paradise filled that room! Having received the last Sacraments, she expects nothing more from the earth, her thoughts turn to Heaven where she beholds the long-desired nuptials; her bed is surrounded by four priests and by the grief-stricken sisters, who can scarcely restrain the anguish of their hearts, and she turned to each a sweet gaze, a kind word, an angelic smile, as if to say: I am going to heaven; I am flying to paradise. And the moment had come. The clock struck half past ten, and she, feeling herself failing, called her spiritual father, and: "Father," she said to him, "commend my soul." These were her last words, like those spoken by Jesus on the cross, and having said this, she expired.

Blessed soul! You flew to heaven, and delight in your God; to us you left the fragrance of your virtues and the longing for you.

Pray now, since you are in the bosom of blessedness, pray for us who sail the tumultuous sea of the world; pray for your holy Institute and for your sisters, while we, imploring God for your eternal rest, offer this tribute of heartfelt praise to your sweet and holy memory."

Meanwhile the funeral was being prepared, which was to prove most moving. To the Reverend Father D. Giovanni Maccatajo was entrusted the task of composing the inscriptions that were to adorn the Chapel, a task he carried out with uncommon love and skill, composing the following epigraphs, which sum up the whole holy life of the lamented deceased:

On the door of the Chapel:

To the blessed soul

of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne

fervent religious

of Sicily and Calabria

meritorious Provincial Superior

at the modest funeral obsequies

which grieve

her dear religious sisters and little daughters

sweet tribute of sincere tears

fervent prayer

of everlasting rest

they offer

Inside the chapel on the right-hand wall:

The grace of God

guided her first steps

in the holy commandments

as a child

she placed her delights

the fleeting pleasures of youth

with firm step

generously she trod

the world Courted her Desired her

but did not have her

Idem

On the happy day

when with a holy bond

she bound herself by religious vows

she was no longer her own

but belonged to the Institute and to her neighbor

apostle of charity

sought everything for others

nothing for herself

angel of comfort

to the sick to the afflicted

to the sorrowing

dried tears soothed sorrows

won souls for God

On the left-hand wall:

Humble modest mortified

what her right hand did

her left hand did not know

amiable sweet kind

whoever knew her loved her

attentive zealous energetic

did everything overcame everything

heroic in obedience in sacrifice

victim of love

suffered everything

serene in soul sweet in face

smiling she looked at death

and peacefully expired

Idem

Ray of heavenly light

which illumines gladdens enraptures

spread its splendors amid the darkness

but by the darkness it was not overcome

lived in the world but not of the world

had on earth exile

paradise in the beloved Institute

and found everything in her God

Blessed soul

you carried your rays elsewhere

and shine in blessed eternity

in the bosom of God

And here it would fall to me to describe the funeral ceremony, to show with how much gratitude, with how much piety and devotion the last tribute of affection was paid, by her most grieving fellow sisters and by the sorrowing people of Palermo, to one who had made her life a continual sacrifice for the benefit of her neighbor, in whom she always saw reflected the image of her Jesus. But, mistrusting my own poor and unadorned words, I refer to what the newspaper La Sicilia Cattolica wrote, which on June 15-16, in its article entitled "Solemn Funeral," gave the following report:

"With most gracious and pious thought, solemn obsequies were celebrated this morning [June 15] for the virtuous and lamented Provincial Superior of the Daughters of St. Anne, in the Oratory of the Central House for Sicily, within the Briuccia Palace.

The said Oratory, and the vast hall preceding it, were elegantly transformed for the occasion into a funeral chapel, its vaults draped in mourning cloth, with mournful veils fluttering on the walls. At the entrance of the Oratory and all around, one could read most gracious epigraphs recalling the eminent and singular virtues of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, and in the center rose a magnificent urn of velvet and gold, with the deceased's photographic portrait, upon whose steps were laid various wreaths, from the Daughters of St. Anne of the Asylum, from others of the Hospital, from those of the Fernandez Infirmary, etc.

One entered that Oratory, and an arcane and mysterious feeling of sorrow and of joy, of death and of paradise, pierced to the heart... and those grieving Daughters weeping around their Mother's bier: and those noble and pious ladies of Palermo coming there to pay the final tribute of admiration to one so dear to them... and the whole of that mournful array, one could not well say whether it turned the mind more to the sorrow suffered, or to heaven, where an angel had flown to pray before God's throne for the Daughters, for the Institute, for Palermo, for the languishing wretched who had been, in this valley of exile, her special delight, and for whom she had a mother's heart, a seraph's charity, the living, ardent, boundless charity of Christianity and its great institutes.

A great number of Masses were celebrated throughout the day in suffrage for the deceased Provincial Superior; and the solemn canonical Requiem Mass was sung by Monsignor Ignazio Zuccaro, secretary to His Eminence the Cardinal Archbishop of Palermo, through whose efforts the blessed Institution of the Daughters of St. Anne became established among us, and does so much good, and promises still finer fruits for the future.

The funeral eulogy was read by the Beneficiary Gaetano Gabriele, who knew how to show, with delicacy, the manifold virtues of Sister Anna del Salvatore under the aspect of the chief among virtues, humility, which inspired her in various ways, thereby pleasing God, and making her a guide, a comfort, a relief to humanity.

The death of the Provincial Superior was a true loss... of that kind of woman and Christian virgin, who loves and prays, who smiles and consumes herself in penance, prudent in governing and loving in guidance, who has the innocence of the dove and the strength of the valiant woman, who lives not for herself but for the suffering members of the mystical body of Jesus Christ. Who did not see her, and did not love her, did not esteem her, was not captivated by her virtue and her manner?

Blessed one! Your daughters will not forget you, this city will not forget you... and pray for us all!

XI. Transfer of the Remains of Sister Anna del Salvatore to the Place of Deposit

Two years passed since the death of Sister Anna del Salvatore, and not only in Palermo but throughout Sicily her memory and that of her virtues remained ever alive. It was the general opinion that Sister Anna del Salvatore was a great Servant of God. Since people spoke of special and extraordinary graces obtained through her intercession, everyone was of the opinion that one day her many merits would be universally recognized, and Sister Anna del Salvatore, who in life had humbled herself, would be exalted. They therefore formally begged the venerated Cardinal Archbishop Celesia to order that the body of the lamented Provincial be placed in temporary deposit, and His Eminence graciously received this petition, he himself holding Sister Anna del Salvatore in great esteem.

In the Cemetery of St. Ursula, then, the pious ceremony took place; and concerning it, here is what the newspaper "La Sicilia Cattolica" said, of February 18, 1877 [sic for 1887], in its article entitled: "Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi and the Institution of the Daughters of St. Anne."

"On the 14th, in the Cemetery of St. Ursula, a sad but at the same time consoling ceremony took place.

Readers will recall, the city of Palermo recalls, that in June 1885 the blessed soul of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, Provincial of the deserving Daughters of St. Anne, passed to eternal rest. Her death was received with great anguish by all who knew her, and a spontaneous cry was heard everywhere: "A Saint has died!"

This cry was taken up by the priests who frequented her, by the families who had the good fortune to be close to her; so that all formally begged our venerated Cardinal Archbishop that, in consideration of the deceased's virtues, he order her body placed in temporary deposit, awaiting the Lord to manifest further the works of His omnipotence.

Our Pastor, without the least hesitation, graciously received this request and, considering the blameless life of the good religious, ordered that her remains be kept in temporary deposit in accordance with the prescriptions of the Holy Roman Church.

And it was in the Cemetery of St. Ursula that this sacred ceremony was to take place. A moving scene! Around the tomb, from which the blessed deceased was to be exhumed, stood: His Excellency the Most Reverend Monsignor Giovanni Cirino, Archbishop of Ancyra and Vicar General of the Archdiocese of Palermo, Monsignor Ignazio Zuccaro, through whose zealous work we have among us the Daughters of St. Anne, the Most Reverend Canon Antonino Calì, Chancellor of the Curia, and many priests. Also present was a numerous company of Daughters of St. Anne accompanied by their venerable Foundress and Mother General, who had come expressly from Rome to testify her affection for the virtues of the deceased; and at the Mother General's side were the Princess of Fitalia and one of the Misses Sorrentino.

We could not say in words the emotion felt at the moment the casket containing the good religious's remains was uncovered. It was weeping mixed with contentment! Around those bare bones, the good Sisters recognized their Superior, who had so edified them with her humble and mortified life; and they recalled, extolling them, her singular virtues, and her tireless zeal for the salvation of souls, and could not help exclaiming: "She was a Saint!" Happy to be able to kiss that hand which had so often blessed them, they were not content with having gazed upon it enough... and the rosaries, and the small crucifixes they wore at their sides, they laid upon the blessed body, almost as if to receive from it some arcane and superhuman virtue in the laborious and yet sweet practice of their Institute's Christian love.

Once the verification of the body was complete, it, together with a parchment (on which the Most Reverend Father Domenico Pizzoli, Parish Priest of St. Nicholas of the Albergheria, had concisely written the story of the life of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi), was enclosed in a new casket with the archiepiscopal seals, and an appropriate record was drawn up of everything. The sad ceremony ended with the bloodless sacrifice of the Mass, celebrated by the Most Reverend parish priest Palazzotto, which those present devoutly attended.

Blessed Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, which already shows us the first fruits of its virtue and its holiness! Surely it is providential in our day, and we are glad to take this opportunity, which has brought the Mother General to Palermo, to bear witness, together with our own, to the applause and blessings of religion and of civil society.

The noble Lady, the Countess [sic] Rosa Gattorno, well understood that woman is made for the great struggles human nature wages against suffering. She therefore fell in love with the blessed Institute, and, leaving behind the splendors of her House, gave herself to the work! And here are the Daughters of St. Anne, in whom the feminine fiber seems to be tempered into valor; and the frail creature, become manfully bold, grows great in courage amid dangers, advances with spirit in life's battles, dies bravely, gloriously, in the face of the hardest trials. Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi is a noble proof and eloquent witness of this. Was she not a victim of her charity?

Even today, the newspaper entitled the Esercito Italiano warmly greets "the angelic Daughters of St. Anne" who have gone to the inhospitable shores of Africa. And we add that they, like soldiers, have a uniform; like combatants, a weapon, the cross; like warriors, a discipline: but if the soldier fights the enemy for the honor of the flag, for the glory his fellow citizens will pay him when, returning victorious, they receive him in triumph, crown him with laurel, and shower his path with handfuls of fragrant flowers; oh, they aspire to no glory on this earth, they have no enemies but human ailments to cure, they consecrate themselves for brothers who, like them, speak the same language, sacrificing themselves also for all those Jesus Christ has redeemed, for all those on whose brow shines the mark of an immortal soul, for they are the soldiers of humanity.

Blessed Daughters of St. Anne! Most noble is the undertaking of charity, it is the great, sublime idea that God Himself brought to earth. If the world sometimes scorns you, that world whose perfidy the unhappy Leopardi understood so well, and noted to be in harmony with what the Gospel says of it... oh, pay no heed to the voices of men, draw your inspiration rather from the magnanimous examples, from the virtues of your Institute. In Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi; let those who succumb in hard trials be succeeded by others, placid and serene as the genius of charity.

From the heights of heaven, Almighty God will bless so many sacrifices and so much heroism, and will mark your Institute with the sign of holiness.

Let us pray the Lord that He may be pleased to glorify His faithful servant, Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi!"

XII. Testimonies Confirming the Virtues and Merits of Sister Anna del Salvatore, the Wonders Worked by Her in Life and in Death, and the Graces Obtained Through Her Intercession

And now that, as best I could, I have spoken of the blameless life and holy death of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, I report some facts gathered from sisters who had occasion to live with her, and I do this with the intention of confirming, with testimonies of unquestionable faith, the truths I have set forth concerning her illustrious virtues. There is very much to learn in the life of this Servant of God; it is good, therefore, that it be told without any willful omission.

Beginning, then, with one of the chief virtues, holy Obedience, here is what is told of an extraordinary nature! It should be known that Sister Anna del Salvatore, accustomed always to eat vegetables, most often spoiled ones, suffered a great deal in her stomach when forced to take other foods. One day the Mother, fearing that with such a way of life the sister would ruin her health, ordered her to eat other dishes. She said not a word and promptly ate all that was set before her; but afterwards she felt so ill that she was forced to vomit it all up. She suffered laughing, for the joy of having done her dear Mother's will, whose wishes were laws to her.

Equal to obedience in Sister Anna del Salvatore was the virtue of humility, about which the following is told: when Sister Anna del Salvatore was Superior in a house where Holy Mass could not be had every morning, she sent the sisters to hear it at church before herself, and meanwhile busied herself with the lowliest tasks of the house, such as sweeping the rooms, making the beds, dusting the furniture.

Every morning it was she who gave the wake-up call; but first she pumped enough water to fill the container, so the sisters would not have to tire themselves fetching it during the day. And on days when there was laundry to do, she washed the linens before the Sisters rose from bed.

Her conferences were often on humility, and she taught the sisters always to regard themselves as the last. She wanted them to go to the table as poor little women going to receive alms, and when she was addressed by the title of Superior, she would answer: "The Superiors of this House are St. Anne and the Blessed Virgin; they alone rule and govern it: I am nothing at all."

Once, before she was yet Superior, Sister Anna del Salvatore went, with the companion who later reported the fact, to attend a poor woman long sick; she was found so filthy as to cause disgust. Well, she went to her, kissed her, and then, with unparalleled humility, cleaned her entirely and kissed her again, exclaiming: "Oh, would that my soul were as clean as this!"

Another time she went with the same sister to beg for alms, and entered the house of certain gentlefolk who, whenever they saw her, heaped scorn upon her. She was treated worse than a dog, but she bore the insults and kept going there every day, exactly as though she were received there with the best of treatment.

In the Community she always showed herself humble and respectful towards everyone; she never asked anything for herself, and when the Superior said to her, "Sister, do you need anything?" "A little love of God, Superior," she would answer.

As for poverty, it is told that Sister Anna del Salvatore paid no heed to her clothing; everything suited her. The more patched a habit was, the dearer it was to her, and the Mother once had to compel her to put on a new tunic, because in the one she had worn for years upon years the patches and mendings lay one upon another. She would have gone with her toes sticking out of her shoes had the sisters not taken care to replace the worn-out ones with a new pair; and it often happened that she did not notice the change, and when she did notice it, she took them off to give to another Sister.

No waste, however slight, would have been permitted: it was observed that, so as not to throw away that little bit of wick cut from a new candle, she made use of it, dyeing it yellow, to make the stamens of artificial flowers. She called herself owner of nothing, considering herself a mere custodian of the Community's goods, and was most jealous of them.

Once she arrived at a House and, laughing, told how she had traveled with her companion in the livestock car because she did not have enough money to lodge more comfortably. She said, however, that she had afterwards met an old man from whom she had received, as alms, 50 lire.

It is impossible to imagine all the affection Sister Anna del Salvatore felt for the Mother. Many sisters attest that when she spoke of her, abundant tears of tenderness ran down her cheeks. She would always have wished to be with her dear mama, as she called her, to venerate her, to kiss her garments, to breathe the air she breathed.

When she received letters from her, she leapt for joy, kissed them repeatedly, and would have wished to write to the Mother every day, because it seemed to her thus to lessen the distance separating her from her.

When she received news that the Mother, whose health was almost always poor, was unwell, she felt such sorrow that she became sad and melancholy, avoided even taking her meager meal of vegetables, and would not return to peace until she had better news.

It was not possible for her to pray without commending to God her dear Mother, and very often she invited the sisters as well to say special prayers for her. And how she grieved whenever she had occasion to discover that in some sister's soul there did not dwell, towards the Mother, all the affection she deserved.

She also bore much benevolence towards her fellow sisters, for whom she was all charity and sweetness. She bore the heaviest burdens of the Community to spare the others. If then some sister was sick, she did not leave her bedside by day or by night; she herself was the nurse: and if another, instead, was troubled by some anguish of spirit, the good Superior consoled her, encouraged her with charity, and she returned to peace. This is attested by a sister who had occasion to experience such anguish.

If the house found itself in straits, she suffered not for herself, who needed little, but for the sisters, to whom she would have wished nothing ever be lacking.

Before dying, she said to a sister who, weeping, stood beside her: "What is it? Be of good cheer." And yet one could see that she too suffered at leaving her fellow sisters; but she sought to console the others, forgetting her own grief.

I reproduce here some passages from the letter of the Provincial Sister Anna del Salvatore, dated May 13, 1885, in answer to the Superior of the hospital of St. Xavier, who, unable to go to her because smallpox had broken out in that pious place and the sisters were therefore under quarantine, and also needing to tell her certain things, had written to her.

"Dearest Superior... Now let us come to you, how is your health? My God, what deep sorrow I feel for you, my good Superior! But courage, for I hope you will very soon be free of it. How are the sisters? Write to me soon about them..."

As for her rapture in holy Prayer, here is what could be gathered.

The Superior, Sister Anna del Salvatore, invited a postulant one evening, secretly, to spend the whole night praying with her before the Blessed Sacrament. The postulant agreed, and they remained in the Chapel until morning, always praying. There are no words adequate to describe her fervor. She often gave forth loving sighs for her beloved Jesus; and the one who was with her thought to herself: "Oh, how devout and absorbed this Superior is!" She was prostrate before the Blessed Sacrament, when she was seen to rise more than a hand's breadth from the ground, then, little by little, return to her knees. Then she hurries to her prayer companion and says to her: "Do you believe that you will soon be a nun?" "Yes, yes, Superior," the other answered her, "indeed, from this night on I swear before the Crucifix, to which she has prayed so much, that I will be the bride of no one but Him alone."

It is repeatedly affirmed that during prayer Sister Anna del Salvatore's face took on the appearance of an angel's, so that it no longer seemed a human thing, but a heavenly one.

There is a sister who attests to having been, in 1877, with the Superior Sister Anna del Salvatore, and that on many nights, around one o'clock, rising to go see where the Superior was, she found her almost always on her knees on the bare ground, leaning with her arms on a chair. She burned with love and shed abundant tears before the Tabernacle, and, being asked repeatedly by the sister to go rest, she answered that it was not late yet, and that she had to stay there to keep Jesus company, who was alone in the Chapel.

In the morning, after Holy Communion, she hid her face in her hands, and however much they called her and shook her, she did not move.

In that same year 1877 (it is still the same sister speaking), one morning the Community had gathered in the Chapel for prayers. At the words: "No, we cannot," etc., etc., the Superior vanished from the sisters' sight. One of them, however, immediately ran to catch up with her; but in vain was she sought everywhere: she was not found until several hours later.

Another time, in 1877, Sister Anna del Salvatore was with the sisters in the parish church of the town, where the house was located, they having no chapel of their own, and shortly after Holy Communion she gets up from the pew saying: "Let us go." The sister next to her also moved, but however much she ran, she could not catch up with the Superior, who, as if she had wings, covers the distance in an instant and, arriving at the House, enters the first room, locks herself in, all in a flash. She throws herself on her knees, her eyes full of tears turned and fixed on Heaven, her arms spread in the form of a cross, speaking a language that the sisters, who are watching and listening through the keyhole, cannot understand. They knock repeatedly on the door, call the Superior, who does not answer. After some time she comes out of the room and seems ashamed to be in their presence, and says she had done one of her usual things, and declared herself crazy, a dolt, without sense.

In any circumstance, and whatever grace she wished to obtain, or whenever the Mother asked her to pray, she immediately turned to the prayer from the Filotea, on page 492: "Here I am before you, O great Queen of Heaven," etc., etc. — and she obtained whatever she asked, and that same day would say to the sisters: "The Mother, or such a person, or we ourselves, have received the grace; let us thank God for it."

In her talks she always spoke of Jesus's love for us; of Mary Magdalene, when she went among the soldiers accompanying Jesus to Calvary and was looked upon and called by name by Jesus Himself. She spoke of Jesus under the figure of a fisherman, and when she saw a fish she would exclaim: "Oh, how I wish I could catch big fish for Jesus!" She was often heard to say: "From the Tabernacle comes a continual voice urging us to love Jesus."

She was many times found in the corridors and in the sacristy, on her knees with arms outstretched, before some image of the Saints, absorbed in fervent prayer, and some times she was also seen, by a sister assigned to give the wake-up call, half-dressed, kneeling at a window from which a small church could be seen, in the act of adoring Jesus in the Sacrament.

And while she prayed she was often rapt in ecstasy. It is told, in this regard, that once, four of the five sisters making up that small Community having gone out to attend the sick, only the Superior, Sister Anna del Salvatore, had remained at home. Returning from their duty, the four sisters repeatedly rang the bell, without its being opened. So they entered the house another way and found the Superior seated in the dormitory, with her work in her hands. She did not move and gave no sign of having noticed the sisters' presence; one of them called her several times, shook her, but it was not easy to make her hear. Finally, as if waking from a daze, she rose to her feet and was most mortified to find herself before them without knowing how the sisters had come in, who at once judged that she had been, at the moment of their arrival, in ecstasy.

Another time, not having a bed to sleep in, and feeling very tired, she was asked by a sister to lie down with her. She accepted the offer out of courtesy; but the sister, waking during the night, heard the Superior speaking with Jesus so fervently that she felt herself carried towards Heaven. The sister keeping her company pretended to sleep, because she knew the Superior would be displeased if she were caught in those raptures of hers.

No less great than her other virtues was, in Sister Anna del Salvatore, that of abstinence; and in this regard her fellow sisters relate that, once, the Superior having arrived from a long journey, they wanted to give her something to eat, since she was still fasting; but she would taste nothing of what had been prepared for her; out of obedience she drank a little wine, which made her feel ill the whole night. She, however, was content to suffer.

Sister Anna del Salvatore took food only every 24 hours. If she was sometimes forced to take a little piece of chocolate, after much suffering she would vomit it up. She held vegetables and greens already spoiled to be delicious and most excellent food, and often related that, at home as well, she liked to eat coal, ash, raw potato peels, cabbage cores, and salad leaves; and then she would conclude, laughing: "I have always been a little creature."

When keeping vigil over the sick, she was ordered to take a little coffee; she obeyed, as always, but made it with the soot she scraped from the pots.

However many feast days there were in the year, she never tasted fruit or sweets, and all the sisters who lived with her agree in asserting that she did this out of abstinence.

To this virtue Sister Anna del Salvatore joined a desire for penance. The more she suffered, the more cheerful and content she appeared. For Jesus, who had suffered so much for her, no suffering of hers, however great, was ever sufficient; and she was often heard to exclaim: "Jesus, let me suffer for You!" It is for this reason that the sisters discovered a small iron chain that served her as a belt; it is for this reason that she almost always wore the hairshirt, consisting of an iron mesh with points on the inside drawing close to one another. This instrument of penance was highly polished from continual use, and the sisters had discovered it as they had discovered other, shorter ones for the thighs. Friday of every week was the day set for this mortification of the flesh, and the sisters who watched the Superior noticed it because, when she rose and sat down, the marks of suffering would appear on her face.

To confirm what has been said in this regard, there is one who attests that in 1877 Sister Anna del Salvatore had an abscess on her arm. The doctor was at once sent for, but before he entered the room she begged the sisters to leave her alone for a moment. These pretended not to have heard and stayed there, suspecting she wished to remove the hairshirt. So it was; before the doctor's arrival, that instrument of penance fell to the floor, and was picked up by a sister, to the Superior's immense displeasure.

Fearing that her body, treated this way, did not suffer enough, and that for her faults far greater penance was needed, she had taken to not sleeping at night; so true is this that she had no bed, and spent the hours of rest in prayer, in work, and in mortifying her flesh with disciplines.

As for the observance of the Holy Rules, it is the general voice in the Institute that Sister Anna del Salvatore was most scrupulous. Not a single point was neglected by her; so true is this that the sisters who lived with her declared that, for them, it would have been an extraordinary grace if they had managed to imitate her.

It is told, among the many facts attesting to Sister Anna del Salvatore's tireless patience, as one of the most important, the following. Once she was away from the city visiting, in her capacity as Provincial, some houses. She returned to the convent where she resided at midnight, without having informed the sisters of her arrival; and so they, not expecting her, had fallen asleep and had not heard the door bell ring; so they did not go to open it. Who would believe it? Instead of insisting on ringing, she remained for no less than five hours, that is, from midnight until the hour of the wake-up call, on the pavement, using her suitcase as a seat and shivering with cold, since it was in the depths of winter. When, after the wake-up call, the sister went to open the door, she found the Superior almost frozen on that uncomfortable seat, and asked her when she had arrived. "At midnight," she answered. "And why didn't you ring?" She said she had rung, but softly, so as not to wake the gentlefolk living in the building. And while the sister was distressed over what had happened, she showed herself most content, because she had had the chance to think of St. Francis, when he too was left outside the convent by his friars, who had not heard him knock at the door. An admirable example of extraordinary patience, of which only a holy soul can be capable!

And being the holy soul she was, Sister Anna del Salvatore also had, like the saints, the grace of discerning the affections of the heart.

In this regard the same sister to whom the event happened relates that once, returning from a night vigil, she felt troubled about making Holy Communion. As soon as the Superior saw her, she said to her gently: "Wait, for the confessor will come later. I have already understood everything; but I don't want to know anything." She had entered into the sister's soul and discovered its secret torments!

Nor are examples of foreknowledge missing from her life, for another time Sister Anna del Salvatore was in Piacenza and, at the moment of the elevation, heard a voice which told her that she would soon go to another house, where she would see a certain person. This indeed came to pass; not much time passed before she was ordered by the Mother to go to that house, where she found the person who had been indicated to her.

When, on a certain occasion, elections for the Town Councilors were to be held in a town, the Reverend Parish Priest had commended the election of good men to the prayers of Sister Anna del Salvatore, who, though no one could know the outcome of the voting, since the counting had not even begun, said with full confidence to her fellow sisters: "Be of good cheer; things have gone well, and the Father's wishes have been fulfilled." That evening the Superior's prediction was publicly confirmed.

Once, Sister Anna del Salvatore went to visit a house. Before leaving, she wished to see the confessor, and, greeting him, thanked him repeatedly. He was astonished and asked her, rather imperiously: "What are you thanking me for?" She did not answer, but already knew, without anyone having said a word to her about it, that this priest, Don Vincenzo Sardi, had had lunch prepared for her and her companions in the town where they were headed. Arriving there, they went to visit the confessor's sister, who lived there, and found the lunch prepared, for which she had already given thanks in advance to the confessor himself.

A week before her own condition worsened, she went to another House to visit a sister who had long been ill, and said to her: "Courage, sister, for you will not die now; but both you and I have little time left to live." So it was; both died on the same day and were laid in the same grave.

On the last day of her life, the Superior asked a sister how certain sick women of the Community were doing, and particularly one, given up by the doctors, who was at death's door. The one asked did not want to say how things really stood, fearing to upset her; but she, as if she had been told the reason for that silence, added: "Have no doubt, sister, that that gravely ill woman will not die; I myself will die, but she will recover, and soon." And so it was.

From prophecies, moving to wonders, we relate first of all what the Provincial Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi attests, who, in dressing the body of Sister Anna del Salvatore, observed a vermilion-colored mark on the side of the heart, and, having been ordered by the Confessor, to whom she mentioned it, to examine it closely, judged that only a supernatural cause could have produced it.

Several well-noted wonders worked by Sister Anna del Salvatore during her life are then enumerated. Here are some of the principal ones.

1. - A sister relates:

"While I was still a postulant, the Superior Sister Anna del Salvatore took me to see an aunt of mine, who gave me an envelope containing 80 lire. As soon as we arrived home, I gave her the lire I had received from my aunt as a gift. She looked at them for a long while, then exclaimed: 'But this is not the money I need; I am short by at least more than double this amount.' Meanwhile she gave me back the envelope with the money and took me to church, where she ordered me to place the envelope, just as it was, behind the Gloria Card, and bade me pray hard. She left the church and left me there alone for no less than two hours. When she returned, she told me to go get the envelope, and oh, wonder! together we counted the money and found it had grown by 200 lire. I was then convinced that the Superior had worked a great miracle, and I was left edified."

2. "Another time, also when I was a postulant, Sister Anna del Salvatore took me by the hand and, smiling, said to me: 'Come, come with me to the little parlor, for I need to write to the Reverend Mother.' She had barely written on the sheet the words — 'My dear Mother' — when she set down the pen on the little table, saying: 'I am so sleepy that I cannot go on writing: I'll stop; half an hour's sleep will be enough for me,' and, resting her head on my shoulders, fell asleep, asking me to wake her soon, since she needed to finish the letter to the Mother. But while she slept, it seemed to me, as I kept my eyes fixed on the sheet of paper on which the letter had been begun, that the sheet was already entirely written. Then, believing myself to be under a hallucination, a dream, I rubbed my eyes thoroughly, but no, I was not hallucinating, no, I had not dreamed, what I had seen was real. Full of astonishment, I woke the Superior and showed her the written sheet, and she, without showing herself amazed by it, said to me: 'Good, good! The letter to the Mother is written, and we have nothing else to do but go to the Chapel to thank the Lord for it.'"

3. The sister of Don Vincenzo Sardi, at whose house, as has already been said, Sister Anna del Salvatore and two other sisters were lodged one day, being about to give birth, was in danger of her life. When the Superior went to her, she was indeed near her delivery, and in the family great fear was felt, for, having had a pregnancy even worse than her previous ones, they held a catastrophe almost certain. The Superior saw her and said not a word to ask how she felt; she accepted the lunch cordially offered her; and, although she knew that food would do her harm, she gave no sign of it, and indeed sternly reproved the sick woman's sister, also a nun, who was with her and who advised her not to eat, knowing how much she would suffer afterwards. The lunch over, she took leave of her hosts, protesting her liveliest gratitude for the welcome received. Well then, to this visit, which that excellent family regarded as a special grace, was afterwards attributed the miracle that Don Vincenzo Sardi's sister, against every dire expectation, gave birth to a fine baby without suffering at all from her illness.

4. In 1877 Sister Anna del Salvatore was Superior in a very poor house, and one day she found herself in great straits, having nothing with which to pay the baker, to whom about 200 lire were owed. She shut herself in her room, where stood the wooden Crucifix the sisters said spoke to her, and prayed at length. Then she went out of the house and received from a lady, as alms, 200 lire, with which she went at once to settle the debt with the baker. Such wonders occurred frequently; suffice it to say that that House began with only two lire and, after some years, found itself provided with all it needed, and able comfortably to support no fewer than 50 permanent sisters.

5. Once she went with a sister to attend a poor dying woman. The Superior, seeing that the sick woman no longer showed any sign of life, had her swallow, as best she could, a little card of St. Anne, and the poor woman, within a few days, recovered her health. St. Anne had granted that Sister Anna del Salvatore should work that wonder.

But not only in life were special graces obtained from the Lord by this good soul. Very many already are counted as having been granted through her mediation from the time of her death to today, and here are the most extraordinary ones known to the Institute:

1. The Community of the Briuccia house finding itself in want, and needing to send some sisters to Naples, the Provincial Sister Anna Battistina ordered the Community to go to the Chapel and entreat Sister Anna del Salvatore to come to their aid in this need. While the sisters prayed, Sister Anna Battistina and Sister Anna Macrina went to Mrs. Florio to ask her favor of four free places as far as Naples. As soon as this wish was expressed, Mrs. Florio had her husband called, and with the greatest ease they granted not merely four but six free places.

2. Sister Anna Caterina died on September 5, 1885, at the hospital of Palermo, and the Superior Sister Anna Battistina had an ardent wish that she not be buried in the ground; but since, according to the regulations, another month had to pass to complete the year since the last deceased sister had been buried, in order to open the family vault, there was much fear of not obtaining this permission. All the sisters of the hospital made entreaties to Sister Anna del Salvatore for this grace, and, despite the difficulties the Municipality usually raises, the permission was granted against all expectation. Everyone, including the cemetery staff, attributed it to a miracle.

3. During the cholera outbreak of 1885, Sister Anna Clarenza, gravely ill with internal consumption, gave cause to fear for her life, already confined to bed with the illness far advanced. Recourse was had to prayers to Sister Anna del Salvatore, and the sick woman was able to get up and render services about the house, the other sisters being extremely busy with the charitable care given to cholera victims. When the epidemic ended, Sister Anna Clarenza had to return to bed. Further prayers were offered that Sister Anna del Salvatore might obtain from God the grace of preserving the sick sister's life until the cemetery where the Daughters of St. Anne are buried should again be opened, otherwise the poor sister would have had to be buried with the cholera victims. Sister Anna Clarenza died on December 13, and the next day, the day of the burial, the cemetery of St. Ursula was opened by order from above. This event was a great consolation to the Community and inspired wonder in everyone.

4. Another sign of protection granted by Sister Anna del Salvatore to the Institute was the following. Great troubles were about to befall the Briuccia House on account of two persons, whose names are withheld, ill-disposed towards the Institute. The whole plot was miraculously thwarted and the danger averted with no harm whatsoever to the Institute, after prayers were offered to Sister Anna del Salvatore.

5. Ninfa Varvaro, gravely ill with hemorrhaging, had been given up by the doctors. The sisters attended her; Sister Anna Battistina, moved by the grief of her uncle, a priest, the sick woman's only relative, placed around her neck the rosary belonging to Sister Anna del Salvatore, charging her to pray with this intention. The sick woman began to improve, and within a few days the sisters no longer needed to attend her. Ninfa Varvaro is ready to attest to this.

6. The same Sister Anna Battistina, during her stay in Terranova, was struck by a femoral hernia and could no longer withstand the pain, accompanied by the most alarming symptoms of approaching death. She commended herself with the liveliest faith to the blessed soul of Sister Anna del Salvatore. Several telegrams were sent to the Mother and to the various Communities: "Battistina gravely ill, perhaps operation, have them pray to Salvatore" — Signed: Elisa — "Continues to suffer greatly, pray hard" — Signed: Elisa — and everyone prayed to Sister Anna del Salvatore to intercede for this grace, and indeed, after every remedy had been exhausted with no result, Sister Anna Battistina kept invoking the soul of Sister Anna del Salvatore, and, having placed with great faith the veil of the Servant of God upon the suffering part, she fell asleep for a few minutes, then suddenly felt as if a knot were loosening and was instantly healed. Sister Anna Battistina is ready to certify this miracle under oath. Witnesses to the illness and the grace were the Superior of the Terranova House, Sister Anna Elisa Corsini, the nursing sister Anna Clelia, Sister Anna Fabiana Orsi, two priest brothers named Solìto of Terranova, and the attending doctors.

7. Sister Anna Cunegonda Benini was gravely ill with a quinsy at the Hospital of Palermo. Doctor Mondini had decided, after treating her for several days, to make an incision. The poor sister was frightened by this and, after the doctor had left, commended herself to Sister Anna del Salvatore, promising her three days of fasting on bread and water if she obtained for her the grace of being spared the incision. The doctor, returning the next day, found any operation useless.

8. Sister Anna Battistina Cusmano, a novice of the Rome House, ill from the first days of her Clothing with a great pain in her belly caused by constipation, suffered continual torments. She took various purgatives with little or no effect. She was seen by the doctor, who ordered other purges, which did no good at all. It was then decided to resort to an enema, but first a new purge was tried, which produced no effect. On his second visit the doctor prescribed a certain purgative water, which increased her pains and her constipation, and produced a great swelling of the stomach, on account of which she could neither eat, nor walk, nor sit. Only out of obedience did she swallow a few spoonfuls of broth. A month had thus passed, and the Reverend Superior, seeing that every remedy had proved useless and that the long illness did not allow the novice to remain any longer in the Institute, she being unable to do what the Holy Rules prescribe and therefore incapable of regular observance, thought the best course, if the Reverend Mother agreed, was to send her back to her family. The Superior was therefore most displeased at having to do this and hesitated to decide. Poor Sister Anna Battistina, on learning of the decision about to be made concerning her, could not find peace; she wept day and night, thinking she would have to leave the Institute, a thing that caused her greater pain than the illness itself; the poor woman wept, not knowing where to turn for help, when a sister, Sister Anna Maffea, suggested she turn with fervent prayers to the deceased Sister Anna del Salvatore. Encouraged in this also by the Reverend Mistress, the novice began a novena, and on the evening of the first day she was able to have a bowel movement without resorting to medicines, and had a very noticeable improvement, and that night, after so much sleeplessness, she slept and had this dream: she saw three nuns of her acquaintance, and one of them asked her why she was crying. "I want to see Sister Anna del Salvatore to ask her a grace." Sister Anna del Salvatore indeed came forward and asked her why she was so distressed and tearful. The novice knelt at the sight of her and told her of the illness she suffered, telling her, however, that what tormented her more than the illness was the thought of having to leave the Institute. "No," Sister Anna del Salvatore answered her, "the Holy Mother does not wish it." And, touching and pressing her stomach: "You have nothing," she added, "be obedient." Having said this, she vanished. Sister Anna Battistina went on sleeping until the morning ejaculatory prayer of the wake-up call; she rose from bed completely well, and from that day had no more trouble. Now she is very well and eats with appetite everything the Community serves. Sister Anna Battistina, swearing this to be the plain truth, gives thanks to God and to Sister Anna del Salvatore, who obtained for her from Him instant healing.

9. Sister Anna Stimate had an ailing right eye and was under the care of Doctor Eugenio Scio. It was a serious, long-lasting condition; but Sister Anna dell'Oliveto touched the sick eye with the photograph of Sister Anna del Salvatore, and it was promptly cured. Eyewitnesses to the miracle are Sister Anna Costanza and Sister Anna dell'Oliveto.

10. The same Sister Anna Stimate had to suffer most acute pains in her feet, an ailment that had caused her much suffering also many years before; so true is this that the Mother, aware of it, had already some years before relieved her of the office of alms-collector. Encouraged by the miraculous healing of her eye, Sister Anna Stimate again turned to the dear deceased Sister Anna del Salvatore, telling her she wanted the grace within the month. And it was granted within the set time. The sister felt no more pain in her feet, and, what is better, she now stands all day, keeps vigil, and can comfortably wear shoes, whereas before she was obliged always to wear slippers. The whole Community is witness to this grace, as to the first.

11. Sister Anna Costanza Cenni was struck by a severe pain in the throat, exactly at the spot where, 12 years before, assisted by Sister Anna del Salvatore, she had undergone an operation. There was great fear that another operation would be necessary, so spasmodic were the pains she suffered. But Sister Anna Costanza, after a day or two of treatment, seeing herself getting worse, thought to place on the afflicted spot the photograph of Sister Anna del Salvatore. She kept it there all night, and by morning the pain had entirely vanished. Witness to this miraculous event is Sister Anna dell'Oliveto, who was present when the photograph was applied to the throat.

12. A young woman from the establishment in Trapani, run by the Daughters of St. Anne, was in the Hospital, gravely ill, indeed at the end of her life. The Chaplain went to her to dispose her to make her devotions; but the poor girl, unwilling, turned her back on him every time he approached. Seeing this, the Chaplain withdrew to the Chapel to give the blessing of the Marian month, since it was May, and left the Superior of the Hospital beside the dying woman. She again tried to induce the sick woman to receive the holy Sacraments, but in vain. Then she thought to turn to Sister Anna del Salvatore, and recited to her an Our Father, and when she finished saying it, turned again to the sick woman, asking her if she needed anything, and received the answer: "Call the Chaplain for me." He, interrupting the May devotions, rushed to her, provided her with all the comforts of our holy Religion, and attended her agony, which lasted no more than three hours. Sister Anna del Salvatore had opened Heaven for her.

13. The Reverend Father Gagliani affirms that he has received so many graces from Sister Anna del Salvatore, and that he has therefore taken her as his advocate and protectress before the Most High. Here are some of them:

14. The mere contact of a handkerchief that had belonged to Sister Anna del Salvatore, and which the Reverend Father had received from the Superior of the Daughters of St. Anne in Palermo, with the dying Presti Giuseppe of Comiso (Sicily), produced his miraculous healing. Presti himself, an organist by profession, declares the following: "I, the undersigned, attest that I was so gravely ill from an abscess on my left thigh that my recovery was almost despaired of. The doctors no longer knew what to do, seeing me so overwhelmed by pain: finally one of them, Professor Romè, decided to operate on me. The operation was indeed performed, but with no improvement; on the contrary, I grew worse; when one day, the Reverend Father Gagliani, passing through Comiso with the Sisters collecting alms for the hospital, entered my house and saw me dying. And there was Father Gagliani, full of faith, taking from his pocket the small portrait of a deceased Sister, named Sister Anna del Salvatore, and saying to me: 'Young man, pray with faith to this little nun, I am most certain that through her intercession you will obtain the grace of the Most High.' All those present knelt and prayed. Finally Father Gagliani passed over my face a handkerchief that had belonged to the aforesaid Sister; then he left. Meanwhile I kept getting worse and worse; every path to safety seemed lost, when the Reverend Father Gagliani came again, after a few days, to see me, and renewed the prayer to Sister Anna del Salvatore, and from that day I began to improve so much that I am now in perfect health, thanks to God, to Mary, and to the Sister's intercession." This declaration, dated September 5, 1887, is signed not only by the declarant but also by the witnesses of the grace obtained, namely: Canon Orazio Callisi — Concetta Presti — Nunziata Casane — Canon Gaetano Gagliani.

15. Agira (Sicily), September 6, 1887. — We, the undersigned, swearing upon the Gospel, attest the following:

Cholera having broken out in Agira, we were called to the Ragonese family to attend two women stricken with cholera. There we found the widow Mrs. Scilla and Antonina Ragonese, both struck down with fulminant cholera, in a state truly cold and collapsed, such as to offer not the slightest hope of life. We hastened to encourage the family and the sick women to turn to the blessed memory of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, with the assurance of recovery if invoked with living faith... We displayed there the photograph of that blessed soul and began fervent prayer. Nothing else was needed: after eight hours, urination resumed, and this twenty minutes after the surgeon, upon examination, had declared such a resumption impossible.
