A remarkable change for the better begins: and within 4 days the sick women leave their beds completely cured, with the firmest conviction of having been healed by Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi. This declaration bears the following signatures: Canon Gaetano Gagliani, Sister Maria Anna del Salvatore Beda, Mrs. Ida Avogadro, Mrs. Diega Tramontana, Mrs. Antonietta Santorio, Mrs. Ardica Nunzia, Mrs. Rosalia Deluca, Mrs. Venturini Elvira, Mrs. Giarrizzo Nunzia, Mrs. Rosa Presti.

16. Agira, September 24, 1887. — I, the undersigned, attest under oath that on September 2, 1887, finding myself afflicted by a dispute that seriously threatened my family's peace, as soon as I turned to the protection of the blessed memory of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, of the Daughters of St. Anne, promising her a Holy Mass, within a few hours I found that matter so resolved that every shadow of dispute vanished, and I returned to calm and peace. — To the glory of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi I give this declaration, written and signed by me — Gagliani Francesco, Dr., son of the late Filippo, merchant.

17. Agira, October 6, 1887. — I, the undersigned, certify the following: Being, in these days, torn with grief because, in my husband's absence, as he traveled through northern Italy, I found my two little daughters Sabatina and Filippina afflicted, the first with a severe irritation of the bowels, the second with a convulsive cough, I invoked the aid of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, whose merit I came to know through Canon Gaetano Gagliani, and at once had my daughters fully restored. In thanksgiving to that holy soul I shall soon see to fulfilling my vows and attesting to this grace under oath. — Sfameli Marietta, merchant of foreign and domestic fabrics.

18. Palermo, June 16, 1889. I, the undersigned, swearing on the Holy Gospel and tacto pectore more sacerdotali, attest the following: In October 1888, in a city in Sicily, while I was engaged in a course of Holy Preaching, a woman approached me seeking comfort, tormented by an illness that seriously threatened her health. Grieved by that harrowing account, I knew of nothing better to suggest to her than to begin a novena of prayers to the blessed memory of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, purifying herself first in Holy Confession and approaching the Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist. She answered that she would gladly do so, and that for a year she had never missed Holy Communion. Well, once that novena had begun, it was not possible for that woman to approach Holy Communion, such and so many obstacles opposed her every morning. On the last day of the novena she presented herself to me, dissolved in tears of penitence, and revealed to me that she had seen in a dream a little nun, who announced herself by the name of Sister Anna del Salvatore, and who ordered her to open her heart at once in Confession and be converted, if she did not wish to succumb to terrible scourges.

Repentant and moved, giving me permission to draw up this declaration to the glory of that blessed soul, she revealed to me in confession:

1. that for seven years already she had belonged to the Masonic sect;

2. that she had abjured the Holy Catholic Religion;

3. that she received Holy Communion in order to insult the most holy flesh of Jesus Christ;

4. that she had the mission of corrupting young women, and especially the Sisters of a religious Community.

She handed over to me the shameful documents of her oaths, the insignia of Freemasonry, and, her soul washed clean in general Holy Confession, she returned to the path of salvation. This I attest under the sanctity of oath, to the glory of that blessed soul of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, whom to my life's last breath I wish to have as my sister and special protectress. — Canon Gaetano Gagliani, Apostolic Missionary of the Most Precious Blood.

19. Sister Anna Quintilla, Superior of the Bregnano House, relates: "One evening in the year 1888, as I was lying down, I felt as though the point of a needle had entered the right side of my chest and, without knowing the cause, day by day the pain, the redness, and the swelling grew to such a degree that I could bear it no longer. The sisters begged me to be seen by the doctor; but I answered them: 'I will put all my trust in dear Sister Anna del Salvatore.' Indeed I began a novena to the Virgin, yes, but I took Sister Anna del Salvatore as my intercessor; moreover I put her portrait on the afflicted spot. Oh, a miracle! After twenty days of suffering, which caused me fever as well, on the fifth day of the novena, behold, a small opening formed, through which the point of a pin could pass, and out came first a few drops of blood, black as coal, then pure water, and day by day the afflicted spot deflated, the redness diminished, and finally it healed perfectly without any doctor's intervention. I still keep the scar, however, and inside it, as a testimony, something like a grain of corn, which however causes me no trouble at all."

20. The same Sister Anna Quintilla gives an account of a second grace obtained from Sister Anna del Salvatore, and here is what she says: "Already by 1884, that is, when I was at the house of Giugliano, I had an intestinal inflammation, which however did not confine me to bed, and, going untreated, it reduced itself to chronic intestinal catarrh. Having moved to the house at Pennabilli, perhaps because of the overly cold climate, as the doctor also told me, this catarrh gave me considerable concern, and, the doctor having ordered me a regimen of meat and wine, foods of which I made very little use, too hastily, my intestines suffered so greatly that, besides the swelling of my stomach, so great it even prevented me from wearing the habit, my feet also swelled, so much so that for more than a month I could not wear shoes. The purgatives were without number, but my intestines no longer functioned at all. The Reverend Mother sent me for a fortnight to Pisa, and there they no longer knew what to do to make my intestines work. Then I said: 'No, I will take no more medicines; instead I will begin a novena to Sister Anna del Salvatore, taking by mouth a thread from her stockings,' and behold a second miracle! On the second day of the novena my body righted itself. Yes, all this I certify to the glorification of dear Sister Anna del Salvatore."

XIII. Conclusion

From what has been set forth in the preceding historical notes on the exemplary life of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, one sees clearly how abundant a grace the Lord was generous to pour out upon this His faithful servant, who knew how to merit it so well that she could serve not only as an example to her fellow sisters, but also shine forth as one of the most beautiful among the gems that crown our Holy Church.

May the Daughters of St. Anne strive to imitate her in all her rare virtues, if they wish to attain possession of the One, True, and Infinite Good to which they aspire.

And you, Sister Anna del Salvatore, chosen spirit, from the Seat of Glory where you live in blessedness, never turn your gaze away from the Institute for which you always felt the deepest affection; pray God to bless it and make it ever prosper, and be yourself a firm and sure guide to your fellow sisters on the path which you walked with such ardor and which led you to the longed-for goal, where you live gloriously in the bosom of God for all eternity; so that they may with you enjoy the Blessedness that will never have an end.

An outline, for popular distribution, drawn from documents existing in the Institute's Archive, presented to the supplementary diocesan Inquiry.

Moving briskly through the life and activities carried out by the Servant of God, this work highlights the spiritual and ascetic path walked by Sister Anna del Salvatore, and the solid and widespread reputation for holiness that has always accompanied her, even after her death.

Sister

Anna del Salvatore Orsi

The Early Years

At baptism she had been given the name Marianna, a name rich in spiritual presage for a life that proved to be straightforward and simple, yet very full.

Marianna was born in Albareto (Parma) on February 22, 1842, the Lord's first gift to the young spouses Angelo Orsi and Domenica Mussi. After her the family would be gladdened by eight more births.

Her parents came from comfortable families, among the most prominent in the village, counting priests and public officials among their members. Angelo and Domenica, however, did not place absolute trust in material well-being: they were deeply Christian and committed themselves to raising their children, educating them in faith, hard work, and sacrifice.

Marianna's childhood was full of affection and marked by the birth of her little brothers and sisters, who, along with joy, also brought a gradual increase in responsibility: as the firstborn, she was for her younger siblings not only a lively playmate but also a point of reference, a caring and watchful sister, and for her mother a valuable help with the household chores that increased as the family grew.

Marianna had a sweet, cheerful, and jovial character, and from her earliest years showed a particular attraction to the things of God.

At only four years of age she received, in the parish church of Borgotaro, from the hands of Monsignor Michele Angelo Orlandi, Bishop of Pontremoli, the sacrament of Confirmation, and if at that time she surprised everyone with a recollection unusual for her age, when she made her first Eucharistic communion at ten she would show a far greater religious maturity and a more conscious fervor.

She eagerly attended the catechism lessons of Don Giovanni Maestri, parish priest of Albareto, and passed on their content to her younger brothers; and she was barely past ten when she also began to help the parish priest with catechism lessons for the little ones, and attended daily Mass together with her mother. Still very young, she was caught several times by her mother praying during the night.

Marianna attended no school at all: in a small town like Albareto it was very difficult, especially for girls, to gain access to a public school, but her father Angelo became her teacher, teaching her to read and write, and this instruction would prove precious to her.

Adolescence and Youth

Marianna matured quickly. At fifteen she was very sensible and already capable of running a household. Her priest uncles, Don Antonio Mussi, parish priest of Buzzò, and Don Luigi Mussi, parish priest of Rovinaglia and later of Valmozzola, vied for her to manage their respective rectories. Marianna spent periods now with one, now with the other, giving an excellent account of herself and winning esteem and affection.

In 1858 her brother Giovanni went to Bedonia to attend the seminary as a day student, and two years later his brother Luigi followed him. Marianna was sent to look after them, living with them in a rented room, and until about 1862 cared for them lovingly.

She was not distinguished from her peers by anything extraordinary: Marianna was a young woman like so many others, who took the Christian life seriously and lived it in a coherent and profound way, yet with great simplicity.

Everyone noticed her goodness and her zest for life, the serenity with which she faced sacrifices and privations, the living faith that animated her daily life. Her friends sought her company: they gladly stayed with her, who had a generous heart, who was so gentle and modest and always cheerful. Sometimes they managed to draw her into small family parties or wedding celebrations where people gathered and danced; but it would then happen that Marianna grieved to the point of tears for having let herself be persuaded to take part in those amusements.

Clothing everything in amiability and naturalness, she adopted a style of austerity and mortification, both in food and in other aspects of her simple Christian life. She attended church beyond the strict obligation; she took part in novenas, accompanied the Viaticum brought to the dying, and was woven into the life of the parish; to do this without neglecting her family duties, she reserved for the night hours the work she had not finished during the day.

Sometimes she had a little free time left that she wished to devote to prayer, but the church was closed; she would then kneel in the courtyard and pray fervently, turned towards the house of God. Her family and neighbors, moved, watched her from a respectful distance, not daring to disturb her.

Meanwhile, the family's financial situation changed. The growing number of children and new needs drove Angelo Mussi to incur debts, to settle which he was forced in 1862 to sell his properties and move to Centovera, in the Piacenza area.

Marianna remained in Albareto with her uncle, the mayor Lorenzo Mussi, then rejoined her family, which now more than ever needed her.

The Hour of Decisions

In Centovera, life for the Orsi family was not easy, and the privations were keenly felt.

To help her parents with a small income, Marianna went to work in service for the Bottego family, a family originally from Albareto, perhaps distant relatives, which also included two priests.

Even in her new residence, the young woman found a way to become part of parish life and became the apostle of the town. Everything seemed to pass serenely despite the hardships, but very soon life had a great sorrow in store for her: on July 9, 1867, her father Angelo died, at only 47 years of age. Thus the family's main support was gone, and besides the grief of the heart, it experienced an ever-harsher poverty. In these painful circumstances, Marianna sustained everyone with her serenity and her optimism grounded in trust in Providence.

For some time, meanwhile, she had been questioning her future. Though she felt drawn to a life dedicated entirely to prayer and works of charity, she would have liked to raise a family. Among the young men courting her was Angelo Zecca, who made her heart flutter... When the young man came forward to ask for her hand, she was inclined to accept and, according to the custom of the time, "gave him hope."

Her inner search, however, was not yet finished: she felt called to a greater love, to a charity without boundaries. Her total and all-encompassing love for Jesus proved stronger. It won out. Marianna told Angelo that from that moment he could consider himself free, since she no longer intended to marry but to consecrate herself to the Lord.

"I Will Resist with the Spirit"

Before revealing her decision to her mother and family, Marianna set out in search of a religious community to join. Someone informed her that an Institute had recently been founded in Piacenza, devoted to the care of the sick, which had given proof of truly heroic charity in caring for the cholera victims of the recent epidemic; they suggested, moreover, that she go to the Alberoni College in the city and speak to Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore, the saint, who could introduce her to the foundress.

Marianna took this suggestion as an indication of Providence and, in a month not precisely known in 1868, accompanied by her sister Veronica, went to the College. The Vincentian missionary Father Tornatore received her cordially. But, observing her slender figure, he thought she was not suited to religious life in general, and still less to the life of the Daughters of St. Anne: good health and a robust constitution were needed to bear the toil of caring for the sick, the vigils, and a life of strict poverty. Marianna had perhaps not expected this difficulty, but with simplicity and firmness she answered the priest's objections: "When I can no longer resist with the body, I will resist with the spirit."

Father Tornatore was struck by this strength dictated by faith and understood that this young woman's decision was not the fruit of mere infatuation but of God's grace. He decided to accompany her to the Mother House, on Stradone Farnese, to introduce her to the foundress and make the proper arrangements.

The meeting was most affectionate. The Servant of God Rosa Gattorno perhaps sensed what treasure the Lord was about to entrust to her and did not hesitate an instant to welcome Marianna, whom she at once called "my little daughter"; her entry into the postulancy was set for the month of November.

All that remained now was to obtain her mother's consent, prepare the documents and a small trousseau, and take leave of her relatives.

Unexpected resistance came from her priest uncles, not over the decision itself, but over the choice of Institute: the community of the Daughters of St. Anne had existed for only two years, had not yet been approved by the Church; moreover, it survived on alms and seemed to offer no guarantees for the future. Marianna, with her usual serenity and firmness, managed to overcome these difficulties too, and at the beginning of September returned to her native village, Albareto, to say goodbye to relatives and friends and obtain from the parish priest the necessary certificates.

To her closest friends, who tried to understand her decision, she confided the small signs that had foretold her future: the delight she felt in prayer, to the point of "finding no consolation in this world" outside of it, the impulse to follow a mortified and penitential way of life, the sense of insufficiency of a human love, however beautiful, attractive, and desirable.

The First Steps in Religious Life

On November 4, 1868, Marianna began her postulancy at the Mother House of the Daughters of St. Anne in Piacenza, a period meant for her first acquaintance with and first approach to community life.

A few months were enough to test her vocation, and both the Mistress and the Foundress recognized her uncommon qualities and virtues; very soon, therefore, she was admitted to the Clothing ceremony.

The rite was set for March 28, 1869, Easter Sunday. According to the Institute's customs of the time, with the religious habit a new name was given: she would be called Sister Anna del Salvatore.

The time of the novitiate, which began with the Clothing, was dense and fruitful for our young woman, who applied herself with every effort to the exact knowledge and study of the Rule that was to guide her conduct. The common opinion was that "there was never a more zealous, prudent, sincere, humble, patient, tireless, and chaste novice than she." Doubts and struggles were not lacking, however. But the awareness of having chosen after mature reflection, prayer, and love for Jesus gave her the strength needed to overcome the difficulties.

She loved prayer, during which she often remained so absorbed that she did not notice what was happening around her; she went with heartfelt joy to attend the sick by day and by night; she showed great practical sense and skill in organizing the household work. None of this escaped the Foundress's notice, and before the year of strict novitiate ended, she sent Sister Anna del Salvatore to serve as a nurse in various communities: Sampierdarena, Genoa, Sestri Ponente. Her skill and delicacy in caring for the sick, her ability to instill confidence and serenity, her preference for the poorest patients or those with repellent illnesses, made her a highly esteemed nurse, and every sick person who had known her or heard of her wanted her at their sickbed.

Among her fellow sisters too there was talk of her conduct, which was edifying without being singular or strange in any way. They particularly admired her great humility, her obedience, her charity towards all, her spirit of sacrifice, her exact observance of the rule. Since sisters always went in pairs to attend the sick, the sisters vied with one another to be her companion. One of them, Sister Anna Paolina Viani, relates:

"It was a joy for me whenever I was assigned as her companion in attending the sick. In her company the hours passed more quickly; neither the weariness nor the sacrifice weighed too heavily. Everything was forgotten just seeing with how much love and charity Sister Anna del Salvatore served those poor sick people, who blessed the Lord for having her beside them. Towards us too, who had been given to her as companions and helpers, she showed great charity and wanted us to rest, especially when there was no great need for both of us to be attending them at the same time; she, however, was tireless and never wanted to rest, and when the sick person did not need continuous care, in those intervals she prayed with such fervor."

The trust the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno had placed in the young nun was thus not disappointed; indeed, it grew ever greater, so much so that the Foundress chose her as Superior to open the house at San Martinello, and after some time, that of Florence.

Superior in Florence

The Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne was expanding rapidly; the Foundress undertook frequent journeys to visit the communities and to handle the Institute's affairs before the competent Dicastery of the Roman Curia. The journeys were long and uncomfortable, and so Rosa Gattorno planned the opening of a house in Florence which, besides extending the Institute's apostolate, could serve as a stopping point on the various routes.

The Bishop of Florence, Monsignor Eugenio Cecconi, approved the project in January 1875, and showed himself pleased at the arrival of the Daughters of St. Anne in his diocese. The search for a house and negotiations with persons who could support the sisters who would attend the sick at home were entrusted to Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega, who had in Florence relatives and family friends influential in the local nobility.

The community arrived in Florence on November 20, 1875, and lodged in a rented place on Via Guelfa. The early days were hard, and the community lacked everything. Distress, along with patience and trust, emerges from the letters that, during this period, Sister Anna del Salvatore sent to the Foundress.

"To my great sorrow," she writes on December 5, "I must tell you that we still have no patients; believe me, my good Mother, that I feel the greatest distress over this. Yesterday, Saturday, I went to see Monsignor Giovannini: he received us with such familiarity, gave us his blessing, and told us to be at peace, that afterwards there would come even too many (patients), so that we would not know what to do... Mother, I have delayed writing to you because I hoped to give you good news, but what can I say, I see that so far I cannot; let us hope all goes well..."

A few days later she reports: "Monsignor (Bishop Cecconi) has not yet sent permission for us to go collecting alms, and besides, it has been raining continuously for three days, so I could not go out because we had no umbrella, but now that his charity has sent us one, I will go to see certain ladies..."

In another letter she writes: "In the cash box there are still 96 lire. Believe me, my most excellent Mother, I do everything I can to economize, but until the Lord moves to pity on this little family of ours, I cannot set anything aside... The sisters are all well and are good, cheerful, and content... I beg you to be at peace, all will go well..."

Not much time passed before help arrived, a sign that people were beginning to appreciate the charity and self-denial with which the sisters served the sick in their homes day and night.

Within a few months the young Superior managed to rent a larger house on Via Faenza, to which they moved on April 8, 1876. Then the community grew and the work expanded: a boarding school was opened that soon flourished greatly, requests for care of the sick increased, and the community welcomed sisters passing through who stopped in Florence on their long journeys. Sister Anna del Salvatore arranged for some sisters to be trained so they could teach the girls of the boarding school; their training was entrusted to Father Ottavio Andreotti of the Pious Schools.

The Courage to Oppose

Among the members of the community was Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi, still a novice, who had an ailment, not serious but troublesome, affecting the lymph glands. Father Ottavio Andreotti pressed her strongly to go be treated at home; he assured her she would return once cured, and obtained permission from the Foundress.

The young woman, thinking it would be a short time, let herself be persuaded and set aside the religious habit, but once among her family she realized that the cure would take much longer. She then became aware of the deception: Father Andreotti's intent was to prevent her from ever returning to the Institute.

A few days later, Cecconi, distressed, returned to Florence to her Superior and begged her to keep her with her, because she wanted to remain faithful to her vocation.

Sister Anna del Salvatore welcomed her as a mother and worked to clarify her situation with Mother Rosa Gattorno. The strictness of the times would not have allowed her to shelter her, but she held that charity came before everything and suffered many setbacks on that account.

The Foundress finally understood that Father Andreotti's harshness was unjustified, and Sister Anna Anastasia was again integrated into community life.

She would become an excellent religious and would hold positions of responsibility. "To Sister Anna del Salvatore," she writes, "I owe my religious life."

The Power of Prayer

From the period Sister Anna del Salvatore spent in Florence, episodes are told that have the flavor of the little flowers (fioretti).

One day in 1876, only a few coins remained in the cash box, and the baker, owed a considerable sum, refused to provide more bread. How could they provide for twenty-two people? Sister Anna del Salvatore went to the church of Santa Maria Novella together with Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi and immersed herself in fervent prayer before the Blessed Sacrament.

Their prayer was interrupted by an unknown lady, who held out an envelope, insisted the Superior take it, but refused to give her own name. They tried to follow her to see where she lived and be able to thank her, but the lady seemed to have vanished. Opening the envelope, Sister Anna del Salvatore found the exact sum needed to pay the baker. Similar episodes occurred frequently, and among her fellow sisters the conviction took root that their Superior was helped in an extraordinary way by the Lord.

Among the girls of the boarding school there was an orphan with only one means of support: a benefactor paid for her board and studies. One day news came of the benefactor's sudden death, and the girl, distressed at finding herself once again alone and without help, made a desperate gesture: she drank water in which she had dissolved a box of matches. Her condition at once appeared most grave, and the doctor and the priest were called. Sister Anna del Salvatore herself was not well and was in bed, in the grip of a high fever; nevertheless, informed of what was happening, she hurried to the girl's bedside and knelt before the Crucifix in a heartfelt prayer. Without the doctor's intervention and without any treatment at all, the girl expelled the poison. She was saved.

Trust and Fidelity Put to a Hard Test

Everything seemed to be going well in the Florence house, but difficulties were not long in coming.

Around the middle of 1877, rumors began to circulate against the good name of the sisters and against Sister Anna del Salvatore, who was their Superior. The confessor wished to transform the community dedicated to the apostolate into an enclosed monastery, and the Superior, who resisted his pressure, was accused of insubordination. The vicar for religious life, Canon Luigi Ciaranfi, was also opposed to Sister Anna del Salvatore, and the negative judgments were reported to the Bishop, who, embittered, was inclined to believe everything said by people who enjoyed his trust. A visit by the Foundress Rosa Gattorno restored calm and all seemed smoothed over, but it was only a pause, and the storm gathered more strongly than before.

The Foundress was confused. She had placed so much trust in the young Superior: must she now reconsider? Were these priests' accusations — which, moreover, were never expressed clearly and concretely — founded? But since in this situation the obstacle seemed to be the Superior herself, she decided to transfer her and replace her with Sister Anna Santina Solenghi.

Sister Anna del Salvatore was sent to Appignano as Superior of that community. The transfer, under these circumstances, made her appear guilty, but with profound humility the sister accepted everything, and although her conscience did not reproach her for anything, she asked forgiveness for the troubles unintentionally caused.

She arrived at her new post on April 24, 1878, and with great serenity devoted herself to the sisters, without letting her inner suffering show. In the letters she wrote to the Foundress informing her of the progress of the community and the work, there is not a single complaint, not a word of recrimination, not a protest of innocence. "I ask your forgiveness for all my error and for so much infamy of mine," she writes the day after her arrival, "and I will weep as long as I live. Accept the most sincere greetings from everyone and from me, the most ungrateful daughter..."

Meanwhile in Florence the sisters' situation had not improved after her departure; indeed, Monsignor Cecconi invited the Foundress to withdraw the community as soon as possible. Mother Rosa Gattorno, grieved by this unjust campaign against her sisters, did everything she could to defend them and get the Bishop to retract his decision, appealing to the cardinal protector Franchi and other influential figures, and achieved her aim: in October Monsignor Cecconi allowed the sisters to remain in Florence.

In August 1878, while the situation was still uncertain, the Foundress — as she usually did every year — gathered the Superiors at the Mother House in Piacenza for the spiritual exercises: among them was also Sister Anna del Salvatore. Mother Rosa thought it right to inform them of the difficult position of the sisters in Florence. Surprisingly, some of the Superiors asked that a radical measure be taken against Sister Anna del Salvatore: expulsion from the Institute; others, however, asked that she be forgiven. All of them, then, considered her guilty.

Sister Anna del Salvatore confided to Sister Anna Costanza Cenni: "I have understood that today they will take the holy veil from me... I will offer no resistance; I will do as Isaac did, who made the sacrifice of his life. I will lay my head on the Mother's knees as Isaac laid himself on the bundle of wood; let her do as she wishes, I will offer no resistance; but if I must leave the Institute, I will try, in my lowliness, to do as much good as I can for the Institute, and if necessary I will even go begging alms to help it."

A large group of Superiors came to Mother Gattorno to avert the measure of expulsion and ask that Sister Anna del Salvatore be forgiven. Forgiveness was granted, and some went to find the sister to tell her the news: they found her in the chapel, absorbed in prayer, serene. Humbly she thanked the Mother and the Superiors, and edified everyone with her conduct.

Not everything, however, had passed.

The time the sister was living through was very bitter: no one seemed willing to believe in her innocence. In Ferrara, where she was sent as an educator, she found a prejudiced atmosphere, and some felt it their duty to correct her, almost to "punish" her. In so much suffering and humiliation, the thought of returning to her family crossed her mind. Her relatives, who knew nothing of what had happened but sensed her grief, pressured her to return to them, even promising to set up a chapel for her at home.

The temptation was strong, but Sister Anna del Salvatore entrusted her own cause to the Lord: He would be the one to make the truth shine forth and bring back peace. The love of Jesus triumphed. It was the hour of a suffering fidelity.

In Palermo

After spending a few months in Ferrara, in November 1878 Sister Anna del Salvatore was sent to Rome to direct the "house for repentant women" opened by Father Antonio Bennicelli of the Ministers of the Sick. Among the community's members was also her sister Veronica, who had just completed her novitiate and was now called Sister Anna Fabiana. The environment was difficult, despite everyone's good will. "Here they blaspheme," she writes to the Foundress on November 18, "here they utter curses, here, finally, they pick fights and come to blows... here I have come to hear things I did not even believe existed... As for me, I deserved worse. However I am content, and if you leave me here for the rest of my life, I will gladly stay..."

Shortly thereafter, however, the community was withdrawn because of difficulties that arose with Father Bennicelli when finalizing the contract. Sister Anna del Salvatore was thus transferred again: in January 1879 we find her in Ovada with the office of nurse, shortly after in Sermoneta, and then in other communities.

Meanwhile the Foundress kept observing her behavior and reflected on what had happened. In such difficult moments Sister Anna del Salvatore had maintained unalterable serenity; she had shown herself profoundly humble; from her mouth no word betraying resentment or bitterness had ever come. All this was a sign of a truly uncommon virtue and of a Gospel life lived with continuity and consistency. The esteem that had been clouded returned stronger than before and came to full admiration.

It is natural, then, that Rosa Gattorno, in assigning some sisters to open a house of home-visiting nurses in the city of Palermo at the invitation of Monsignor Celesia, future cardinal, chose as Superior of the community Sister Anna del Salvatore.

The Daughters of St. Anne arrived in Palermo at the beginning of May 1880; not yet having a house of their own, they were lodged by Giacomo Cusmano, future Blessed, who made available some rooms in the house of the nascent Institute of the Servants of the Poor, called "Boccone del Povero," in Piazza San Marco.

Sister Anna del Salvatore writes to the Foundress: "... We arrived in Palermo where we were received very well and with such courtesy that I cannot express it; an excellent lunch; the house is most gracious: magnificent beds, refectory, kitchen, parlor, etc. In a word, we lack nothing. Jesus and the Holy Mother (St. Anne) are with us, so rest assured that with your prayers we will do everything well... Father Zuccaro is in the countryside at Bagheria with the Archbishop and will not be able to come before Thursday evening. So be at peace, my good Mother, for we are in a true earthly paradise."

The sisters immediately began attending the sick, but it took some time before the work took root, and despite the help of the Archbishop and some priests, poverty made itself felt.

"For now," Sister Anna del Salvatore writes to Mother Rosa Gattorno, "Father Zuccaro sends things every day: a dresser, a clock, a table, a washtub; then today I went to fetch 14 crates of fabric for curtains, by order of Father Bova..." And on another date: "As for the care, it goes very well because there is no shortage of sick people, day or night, and they are so content it is hard to believe... As for providence, so far I have still not been able to go out (to beg alms) because Monsignor has not yet arrived." "There are sick people, but so far they are all poor, so we have not received any alms."

Sister Anna del Salvatore did everything she could to ease the sisters' hardships: she was first among them to keep vigil over the sick; she reserved for herself the heaviest household tasks, doing them even at night, so that in the morning, when the sisters rose, they found the laundry nearly all done, or at least the tubs ready, the water drawn, the house clean.

Since care for the sick, according to the Institute's rule, was entirely free of charge, she herself went about collecting alms to support the community; her gentle manner, her jovial bearing, her profound humility won over the hearts of all who approached her, but it was above all the fragrance of Christ's charity spreading around her, imperceptibly but unstoppably, that stirred admiration; and very soon the whole city of Palermo was won over by her.

In Search of a House

About two years after arriving in the city, Sister Anna del Salvatore was still looking for a house. The negotiations conducted by Princess Emilia of Fitalia, who had become a great friend and admirer, dragged on.

With the boldness proper to one who trusts in Providence, Sister Anna del Salvatore presented herself to Monsignor Briuccia, a rather wealthy priest, and asked him for the use of one of his properties. The account she gives the Foundress is simple and spontaneous: "Here I am to give you rather good news of our house in Palermo. First of all, I tell you that the day before yesterday I went to see a great gentleman. I asked him to give us a place for two or three years, or at least until we had provided for another, larger one, and he said these exact words to me: 'Yes, gladly, but only until the end of August; however, now, before you leave, go see the Monsignor Archbishop, and then I will go too, to let him know.' So I did: before leaving I went and told him everything. Monsignor, quite pleased, said to me: 'Yes, let him come see me and we will settle everything.' Indeed he went. I also went to see the Princess of Fitalia, and she told me they are negotiating to buy us a place called San Giuseppe, which belonged to the Benedictine monks, but this will take a while before they get it free. So what do you say? Should I accept the one from Father Briuccia while they buy us that other one? This morning, then, I went to thank him, and he received me with double warmth and told me that Monsignor wants him to give us the place not until the end of August but until the following August, and then... So he, when he saw how willing and attentive Monsignor is towards us, gives us the house rent-free; not only that: he told me that everyone, both the porter and the other servants, will be at our command, and that from today he gives us the keys... What do you say? Should we go there?..."

The Foundress's answer was affirmative, and the sisters moved into the Briuccia palace on Via dei Cinturinai. The large, spacious rooms were a true blessing from heaven, since requests for care of the sick were becoming ever more numerous, and it was necessary to increase the number of nursing sisters to meet so many demands. Sister Anna del Salvatore was pleased that the requests came from both rich and poor, because "it is a sign that the sisters are making themselves loved and are fulfilling their duty."

Shortly thereafter the sisters were requested from various localities in Sicily as well, and for other works in Palermo itself. The Foundress charged Sister Anna del Salvatore with conducting negotiations, handling the opening of new houses, and also visiting those already existing on the island.

Provincial Superior

In May 1884 the communities of Sicily were constituted as a Province, and Sister Anna del Salvatore was named Provincial Superior: thus, with a more official character, the mission she had in practice already been carrying out continued. She directed her own community and inspired all the others in Sicily.

Palermo, Termini Imerese, Agrigento, Castelvetrano, Castiglione, Linguaglossa, Gela, Sciacca became witnesses to her tireless charity, her wisdom in governance, her maternal gentleness towards the sisters and towards the suffering.

What happened once in Castelvetrano is telling: during a visit to the hospital, she found a poor woman, already dying, who earnestly commended herself to her prayers to obtain healing. Sister Anna del Salvatore remained silent for a few moments, then invited the sick woman to think instead of eternal salvation, since there was no hope of physical healing. For two days she then attended her with great charity, comforting her in every way, and also managed to persuade her to receive the holy Sacraments; the woman finally died at peace. Only afterwards did the sisters learn that the poor woman had not approached the Sacraments for many years.

Her arrival at the communities often became an event that involved the whole town. Everyone who approached her was struck and considered her a saint, and vied with one another to have her as a guest in their own home, even for a short time.

Of her serene acceptance of the unexpected too, a charming episode, among others, is told. Once, returning from a journey, she arrived home late at night; she rang the bell, but none of the sisters woke. The Provincial waited patiently, exposed to the winter cold until morning, when Sister Anna Paolina Viani, opening the door, found her sitting on her suitcase, which served as her stool, utterly frozen. They almost forced her to go to bed to warm up, and she, with simplicity and unconcern, told them that all night she had meditated with St. Francis on perfect joy...

If the office of Provincial increased her responsibilities and her external activity, it did not change her austere way of life: she took only one meal a day, of the strictest abstinence, sometimes preferring scraps on the pretext that other foods harmed her health, and she practiced various penances; she spent whole nights in prayer, remaining absorbed in God; if she needed a little rest during the night, she would lie down on the altar step: she had given up having a room and a bed of her own.

Mother Rosa Gattorno followed, moved and admiring, her swift progress on the path of Gospel perfection, rejoicing to see that she had attained a high degree of union with God and that she was enriched with so many gifts of the Spirit; she often entrusted herself to her prayers for the Institute's needs and to obtain graces, certain that her prayer was dear to the Lord.

In a letter from 1884, Sister Anna del Salvatore reassures the Foundress: "I have just received your distressing letter, in which I learn what you tell me about your brother.

My God, what a sorrow! but your sorrow pains me even more, my Mother. Yes, unfortunately everything is true, but I assure you, in the name of the most holy Virgin, that your brother will not die, no, and indeed I hope that the most holy Virgin will not even let him fall ill, and if he does fall ill he will recover soon, yes, soon... and one "no" from Mother Mary is worth more than a hundred demons; so take courage, for all will go well.

I beg you not to grieve, because dearest Mary is already pleading, and Jesus grants her everything..."

In Palermo Sister Anna del Salvatore had by now become a point of reference: Cardinal Celesia made use of her for delicate missions to women's communities, numerous people of every class, and also clergy and religious, turned to her for advice. In a letter from 1884 there is a reference to a foundress: "Yesterday the Foundress of the nuns of the Sacred Heart came to see me... she told me she would like to come to Rome but could not be accompanied because she cannot pay for the journey for two, and if you think I should bring her along when I come, I could bring her. Poor thing, how many troubles! she is truly under the yoke of the greatest tribulations; she has come to see me several times. It is already 28 years since she founded it; she is truly good, already held to be a saint; she would like to go see the Holy Father but wants to speak with you first, Mother..."

Self-Giving to the End

Throughout her whole life, Sister Anna del Salvatore never spared herself. Work, toil, vigils, penances had undermined her physical health but not her cheerful, open character. And she went on spreading serenity, joy, optimism, and courage, even when she noticed her health was rapidly declining.

She felt unwell with increasing frequency, but carried on with her activities as if nothing were wrong, and did not even consider it necessary to inform the Foundress. And so one day in May 1885, while a high fever confined her to bed, she received a telegram from the Foundress ordering her to go to Trapani on an urgent matter of the recently opened community. Sister Anna del Salvatore, who did not yet realize how serious her condition was, ignoring the fever, left at once; in a single day she dispatched her task, but returned to Palermo exhausted.

Her condition at once appeared most grave, and the doctors despaired of her recovery. For her part, Sister Anna del Salvatore understood that her laborious day's journey, although she was only a little over forty, had come to its close, and prepared for death with great serenity, regarding it as the passage from earthly existence to full life with God.

Forgetful of herself even in her suffering, she was concerned about her fellow sisters, was affectionate with them as always, showed lively gratitude for every attention given her, and prayed, prayed unceasingly.

News of her illness spread rapidly through Palermo, and there was a continual flocking of people of every class, eager for good news of her.

One of her fellow sisters, Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, undertook to inform the Foundress, and then something surprising happened. The Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, deeply grieved at the imminent loss of this daughter, wished to make her fellow sisters see how deeply rooted Sister Anna del Salvatore was in virtue and obedience, to the point of heroism; she therefore ordered her by telegram to rise from bed and take part in Mass with the community, receiving Communion in the chapel. The sister obeyed, and the fever left her as if by magic. With another telegram she answered the Foundress saying she was "a little better" and thanked her for her prayers. It was May 28. For a few more days she took full part in the community's life, and the doctors, pleased, thought a recovery was near, but Sister Anna del Salvatore had no illusions: with great effort she took the food ordered for her, and let slip some expression alluding to her imminent death. The sisters of the community, used to her playful manner, paid it no heed; but very soon peritonitis developed in her, and the sister was reduced to the point of death.

On the morning of June 7, she herself asked to be brought the Viaticum, which she received with joy and the greatest devotion; the Anointing of the Sick was then administered to her. She spent her last day in prayer; she gathered her few remaining strength to ask forgiveness of her fellow sisters and to urge observance of the Rule.

She fell asleep in the Lord at 11:00 p.m. on June 7, 1885, repeating the names of Jesus, Joseph, Mary, and St. Anne.

The Lamp Does Not Go Out

After her death, Sister Anna del Salvatore continued to illuminate everyone with her example and her charity.

The newspapers of the time called her a rare woman, a perfect religious, and wove her praises.

In a Circular Letter, the foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne, the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, and the co-founder, Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore, write: "Among all (the sisters who died in 1885) Sister Anna del Salvatore deserves special mention, a truly chosen soul who in life and in death was the admiration of all Palermo... in her all virtues shone forth."

The memory of these virtues remained so alive, the graces attributed to her intercession so numerous, that they led Rosa Gattorno, with her Council, to ask the Archbishop of Palermo that Sister Anna del Salvatore's body be formally recognized in canonical form. The letter of petition recalled "the spirit of prayer and union with God which raised her to the highest contemplation, her simple and profound humility, her spirit of penance, her ready and tireless charity in attending the sick of every kind, her kindness towards her fellow sisters."

Some years later, several bishops, numerous priests, and laypeople of Palermo signed a petition for the opening of the informative process on her life and virtues and on the graces obtained through the intercession of Sister Anna del Salvatore. The process began on September 2, 1896.

*

The fame of Sister Anna del Salvatore's charity and virtues crossed the boundaries of Palermo and Sicily and outlasted the passage of time, reaching us more than a century after her death.

Her simplicity, the truthfulness of her life, her unsparing self-giving for those who suffer constitute a strong call to the Gospel and lead us to reflect on what is truly essential in life, for we shall be judged on charity: "Whatever you did for the least of my brothers, you did for me" (Mt 25:40).

I, the undersigned, Fr. Giorgio Scimeca, archiepiscopal delegate for the cause of canonization of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, Daughter of St. Anne, born in Albareto (Parma) on 2.22.1842 and died in Palermo on 6.7.1885,

declare

that on the 11th day of May 1999, together with the Promoter of Justice and the acting notary, I visited the tomb of the said Servant of God, located in Palermo in the cemetery of St. Ursula.

It bears simple floral decorations, atop which a cross is set; on the front side is a half-bust photograph of the Servant of God. The dimensions of the said sarcophagus are 80 cm in length, 100 cm in height, and 50 cm in depth. The urn rests on a base of dark marble, 80 cm high, on the front of which the following inscription is engraved:

SR. A. DEL SALVATORE ORSI

on the Session of the Historical Consultors

held on September 25, 2007

Rome, 2007

In the afternoon hours of September 25, 2007, the Most Illustrious Historical Consultors gathered in the great Congress Hall of the Congregation for the Causes of Saints, to discuss the Cause: Panormitana, Beatificationis et Canonizationis Servae Dei Annae a Salvatore (in saec.: Mariae Annae Orsi), Sororis professae Congregationis Sororum Filiarum a S. Anna (1842-1885). Positio super vita, virtutibus et fama sanctitatis, Romae 2007. P.N. 2074.

The session, beginning around 5:00 p.m., ended around 6:00 p.m. Besides the General Relator and Relator of the Cause, and the Collaborator, the Most Illustrious and Reverend Monsignor Leonardo Flisikowski, the following Consultors took part in the session: the Reverend Fr. Prof. Marcel Chappin, S.J., Prefect of the Archive of the Secretariat of State; the Reverend Fr. Prof. Vincenzo Criscuolo, O.F.M. Cap.; the Reverend Fr. Prof. Carlo Longo, O.P.; and the Most Illustrious and Reverend Monsignor Prof. Giovanni Maceroni. The Most Illustrious Consultors Prof. Pietro Borzomati, still on holiday, and the Reverend Monsignor Mario Sensi, obliged to attend a scientific congress, were absent. Both had sent in their votes, which were, moreover, favorable.

As is customary for work of this kind, the Consultors were invited to give their reasoned judgment, on the basis of the following questions, using the traditional formulas: affirmative, suspensive, negative.

I. An pervestigationes documentorum ad illustrandam vitam et operositatem servae Dei Annae a Salvatore rite ac plene peractae sint?

II. An documenta collecta et in positionem inserta fidem historicam mereantur?

III. An in eisdem documentis ea inveniantur elementa quae solidum fundamentum historicum afferant ad iudicium de fama sanctitatis servae Dei atque virtutum exercitio ferendum?

In this Positio, the General Relator, Friar Ambrogio Eszer, as in other "positions," appropriately presents the content of the text with references to the collaborators and to the vast documentation. This is an extensive and significant work, without which the Consultors could not have undertaken a serious study. We must, however, also be grateful to the late Monsignor Cataldo Naro and to Sister Roberta Frati, members of the Historical Commission, who offer careful reflections that, in many respects, have been thoroughly evaluated by the competent bodies and by the scholars of the Congregation to which the Servant of God belonged.

In the Informatio of the cited Positio it is asserted that "as noted above, the Blessed Eucharist was her chief devotion, and all her other devotions were subordinate to it. Sister Anna del Salvatore spent every moment left free from her occupations at the foot of the altar before the Blessed Sacrament." Her great devotion to the Pope and to the ecclesiastical Hierarchy was well known. She was distinguished "for her reverence and care for sacred things." In reality nothing distracted her from giving herself to God, whom she invoked in order to attain Paradise. There are, in fact, testimonies attesting to this living with God in love and in order to obtain eternal life.

Fittingly, she practiced a profound faith that was realized in giving herself to the service of her neighbor and — as Sister Anna Elisabetta Veronesi wrote — "one could truly see that it was her delight to serve the sick, in whom she truly recognized the person of Jesus, and she always preferred the poor." It is not an exaggeration, then, to say that she loved the poor with "a maternal love, and showed them the most delicate care."

All this without even mentioning that, precisely because of this overflowing love for her neighbor, "she never deceived anyone."

It has been written that "she loved poverty," and did not fail to be the last; also within her religious congregation, in fact, she chose the most modest things for her sustenance. She was distinguished for her chastity and always considered herself the least of her fellow sisters, offering examples of obedience, obviously above all towards her superiors, whom she considered to be the "voice of God."

The Positio dwells on the "supernatural gifts" of Anna Orsi, describing various circumstances that, before and after her death, demonstrated her truly remarkable reputation for holiness. For these reasons — the Positio notes — "holiness is, for Sister Anna del Salvatore, the only pursuable goal. She wishes to be, herself, a holy nun, but she also wishes her fellow sisters to be holy, as well as all the sick and the people who came near her."

This way of life of hers confirms a Christocentric spirituality, but also a conviction that would have fruitful results, before and after the Second Vatican Council, in papal documents and in the Church's pastoral activity regarding the invitation to pursue a state of authentic perfection, that is, holiness. For this reason the message of the Servant of God has today its own relevance in the Church, a pilgrim in the world and intent on proclaiming the Gospel of Christ.

The Summarium, moreover, bears witness to the various stages undertaken by the Servant of God to attain holiness; she — "always kept fixed in her mind the thought of God's presence in whatever action she performed."

The examination of the content of the witnesses' depositions confirms the judgments expressed about her spirituality, her life, and her works.

Having examined the Servant of God's letters, I fully share the reflections on her personality and other writings contained in the Positio which — as Don Rosario La Delfa, first theological Censor, observes — "from the letters there immediately emerges, with striking consistency, a clear and open character surrounded by a rare blend of optimism and realism." Don Antonino Raspanti, also a theological consultor, significantly wrote that "the Servant of God, from her youth, knew the taste for prayer, which became the inexhaustible wellspring of her life, to the point of being unable to resist the Lord and of finding no more consolation in this world."

It must be kept in mind that Maria Anna Orsi, as has been mentioned, devoted her life to the service of the marginalized; this was likewise the commitment of other consecrated institutes, which operated with difficulty in a context different from that of the country's more developed regions; they, in fact, often performed a role in place of the State's institutions, but also of no few confraternities, the Catholic movement, and other societies of Christian inspiration, which lacked the "gift" of drawing on the spirituality of personalities such as, precisely, the Servant of God.

For this reason, in our own times, Anna can only be held up as an example to the Church and to society. She belonged to a southern Congregation and had no few opportunities in choosing her "service," while the laypeople present in the places where she worked remained indifferent to the perpetuation of abuses against the disinherited, to whom the Servant of God gave her whole self with love, humility, and solicitude. Fr. Dalmazio Mongillo wrote: "The experience lived by Sister Anna del Salvatore is confirmed by all those who, having given everything, wonder how this is possible and where that strength came from which keeps them from stopping and which constantly regenerates itself, in the same way as mercy, which grows when it is received and shared." The biography written by Count Ludovico Masetti Zannini is a decisive part for the careful study of the Positio.

The documents attesting to the Servant of God's industrious life have been the subject of research that can be called thorough, as it allows us to discover Anna's inner richness and dwells on her spirituality, which fed her great love, above all for the poor.

In my judgment the documentation is authentic and exhaustive; it is therefore possible to reconstruct the life and works of the Servant of God. A life distinguished by its identification with those who suffered persecution, predominantly social, and who were forced to lead a hard life, always in vain pursuit of justice.

Undoubtedly notable was, and is, the Servant of God's reputation for holiness; her virtues were, and are, known to all.

For these reasons, I answer affirmative to the questions of the Most Reverend General Relator.

Biographical Profile

The Servant of God was born in 1842 in Albareto, province of Parma, Diocese of Pontremoli, the daughter of small landowners with a house and some fields. Napoleon Bonaparte's widow, Marie Louise of Habsburg, was still reigning! One can imagine the narrow world in which the girl grew up: in a large family (she is the firstborn of eight more siblings); the environment was limited to a small hamlet where the houses were simple; life was austere and frugal; there was always the threat of illness, including epidemics; the schooling situation left much to be desired; religion marked everyday life. Both on her father's and her mother's side, there were priests generation after generation.

The Servant of God received Confirmation at only four years of age; she would also have been admitted, at a young age, to First Communion, contrary to the customs of the time. There are testimonies (Biography, pp. 52-53) of her exemplary life in the family. As the eldest, it fell to her to contribute to her siblings' upbringing — showing firmness when necessary. She also helped with fieldwork. In her small village the memories of her devotions during these years have endured (Biography, pp. 53-55). Her schooling was rather scant.

At about 13 years of age she went to care for her two priest uncles, taking charge of their respective rectories. Later — in the years 1858-1862 — she took material care of two brothers attending the seminary in Bedonia as day students. She continued such tasks for a family in Centovera, in the Piacenza area (where in 1864 her parents had moved because of financial troubles). The young Angelo Zecca hoped to marry her, but the Servant of God — who for some time gave him a degree of hope — decided to consecrate herself to God, a vocation matured over the years. She had to overcome the opposition of her priest uncles (who harbored a certain skepticism about the stability of the Institute) in order to enter the Daughters of St. Anne in Piacenza — she entered the Postulancy on November 4, 1868. She was 26 years old. The Institute was of recent foundation: December 8, 1866! Its foundress is (the future Blessed) Rosa Maria Benedetta Gattorno, widow Custo; Father G.B. Tornatore of the Priests of the Missions is considered its co-founder. The charism was care for the sick (primarily in their homes) and rescuing poor and endangered young women.

After having worked — exemplarily, according to the testimonies — especially as a nurse in various houses (in Sampierdarena near Genoa, where she also served as Superior, in Genoa itself, in Sestri Ponente, in San Martinello, province of Perugia), she arrived in Florence on November 20, 1875, as Superior. The community found itself in a difficult situation; the Servant of God had to face various problems. In Florence the Servant of God underwent a very harsh trial. Relations with the Florentine clergy were already deteriorating. A strong conflict arose especially with Canon Luigi Ciaranfi, vicar for religious women: the Servant of God refused to turn the community into an enclosed convent. The jealousy of the Monsignor towards the regular clergy also played a part (in this case the Piarists, who in the person of a Father Ottavio Raffaele Andreotti [sic] had charge of the sisters). The Servant of God was reproached for not having consulted the vicar for religious women (on p. 158 of the Summarium there is a brief explanation: the Institute — having received the Decretum laudis in April 1876 — could depend on the diocesan Ordinary only for the simple apostolic activity, since its internal order and administration were reserved to the Holy See. The Community's confessor and the vicar for religious women did not understand this distinction. At first even the Bishop did not understand the situation and wanted to close the House; afterwards, better informed, he revised his opinion). There were problems over the choice of confessors. One was imposed who was by no means favorable to the Institute! It reached the point of accusing the Servant of God of insubordination; a defamatory pamphlet was published; she was held to be a liar, and other accusations were leveled at her. The defamation came from a fellow sister. In 1878 she was replaced as Superior and left Florence. A troubled period followed. The Servant of God spent some months in Appiano, then went to Piacenza. Her expulsion from the Institute was threatened (many sisters held her responsible for the difficult situation that had arisen in Florence) — she bore this humiliation with a Christian spirit. In the end she was allowed to stay, thanks to the intercession of a certain group of sisters. Mother Rosa, for her part, declared that the Servant of God bore no blame whatsoever. She was assigned to other communities, sometimes also with the office of Superior. Rome (November 1878 - January 22, 1879), Sermoneta (January 22, 1879 - [probably] June 1879), Ovada (June 1879 - May 1880). On May 2, 1880, she arrived in Palermo: thus began the "Sicilian" phase of her life. She became Superior of a community of "home-visiting nurses." The Institute at that time had 5 houses on the island; within three years another 15 (!) were added. (In the period from 1876 to 1899, a total of eighty houses and one novitiate were opened!). The Servant of God served as Visitator of them in 1883, becoming the following year Provincial Superior of the newly erected Province of Sicily. These were difficult years, also because of her state of health. On June 7, 1885, she returned to the House of the Father, at only 43 years of age. The people's grief was great.

It was, then, a brief life, full of trials and privations.

History of the Cause

In 1894, the Cardinal Archbishop of Palermo received a petitionary letter for the introduction of the Servant of God's Cause, signed by 60 religious and civil figures, among them 3 bishops and 33 priests.

In 1896 the Ordinary Informative Process for the Cause of beatification and canonization began, which dragged on because of various interruptions. In 1907 it reached the 24th session. One would like to know a little more about these delays.

Then 88 years passed, until — in 1995 — the Process was reopened; after 37 sessions, with the examination of 26 witnesses, it concluded in 2000. One factor that delayed the resumption was the introduction of the Cause of beatification of the Institute's Foundress, Anna Rosa Gattorno, in 1912; her ordinary process in Rome closed in 1927. Her beatification took place on April 9, 2000!

A Rogatory Process before the Curia of Pontremoli, begun on January 5, 1898, left no trace whatsoever!

The Research

The report of the Experts "in re historica" (Summarium, 284-296) briefly presents the research carried out.

The archives consulted number 14; the results (including the negative ones!) are briefly indicated; curiously, no mention is made of the Archive of the Curia of Palermo, although it was consulted according to the list on p. 135...

Belonging to an Institute makes it possible for its archive to contain abundant and relevant material, as in the present case.

Contents of the Material

There are the six testimonies of the Ordinary Process of 1896; one might say: "only" six, filling 43 pages. It must be noted, however, that these are highly valid testimonies, confirmed by a considerable number of written accounts by people who had known the Servant of God personally; these are at least 40 written accounts (Summarium, pp. 312 ff.).

There are the 26 testimonies of the supplementary diocesan Inquiry: these are witnesses de auditu (18) or de auditu a videntibus (8). This material is important for establishing the reputation for holiness.

There is a good number of "personal" documents; in order to reach a judgment on the so crucial Florence episode, the Positio offers the Consultors a selection of 28 documents (covering the period from June 30, 1877, to October 24, 1878).

One wealth of material is the Servant of God's correspondence: 349 letters; the Positio publishes 78 of them (Summarium, pp. 189-278).

The Documented Biography drafted by the Most Illustrious Professor Count Gian Lodovico Masetti Zannini is presented as a solid and valid instrument for placing the events of the Servant of God's life in their historical setting.

Conclusion

The good structure of the Positio, the abundance of material — although I would have liked to read a bit more about the history of the Institute (for example, the trend in vocations) — and, I would say, the luminosity of the Servant of God's person, make it easy to reach a conclusion. To the three customary questions I give a positive answer.

Submitted for the examination and judgment of the Historical Consultors is the Positio super vita, virtutibus et fama sanctitatis of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore, born in Albareto on February 22, 1842, and died in Palermo on June 7, 1885, a nun of the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne since 1869. This was a recent Congregation, founded only three years earlier, in 1866, by Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno, who was enrolled in the register of the Blessed by Pope, Servant of God, John Paul II on April 9, 2000.

As is customary, before formulating the judgment on the Positio, which is set out in the answers to the questions proposed by the Most Reverend General Relator, it is thought fitting to present a brief outline of the Servant of God's biographical course, briefly illustrate the contents of the Positio, and make a few observations on it.

Brief Biographical Profile

The eldest daughter of Angelo and Margherita Mussi, the Servant of God was born in Albareto, in what is now the province of Parma, on February 22, 1842; she was baptized the following day in the parish church of the village and received the sacrament of Confirmation on July 26, 1846, at a little over four years of age, according to the normal customs of the time. She spent her youthful years in the family, residing, among other places, with two priest uncles, Don Antonio Mussi and Don Luigi Mussi, whose respective rectories she cared for, and later, from 1858 to 1862, looking after two brothers who attended the seminary. For two years, from 1866 to 1868, she served the Bottego family, in whose household there were two priests. Having lost her father on July 9, 1867, she had decided to become a nun, but in September of the following year she had to overcome the opposition of her uncles, who initially did not approve of her decision to enter the new religious family recently founded by Anna Rosa Gattorno, whom the Servant of God had met shortly before in Piacenza.

On November 4, 1868, Marianna Orsi entered the Piacenza postulancy of the Daughters of St. Anne, taking the habit on March 28 of the following year and also assuming the new religious name of Sister Anna del Salvatore. Perhaps already in the course of 1870 she was sent to work as a nurse in the houses of Sampierdarena, Genoa, and Sestri Ponente. After making her temporary profession on July 26, 1873, she was sent as Superior first to the Orphanage of Sampierdarena, then to Sestri Ponente, and in November-December 1874 to San Martinello, near Perugia. From November 1875 until August 1878 we find the Servant of God in Florence, where she was unjustly held responsible for certain serious mishaps, so much so that her expulsion from the Congregation was feared as an extreme remedy.

Fully rehabilitated, she was sent in November 1878 to Rome, then in January of the following year to Sermoneta, and in June to Ovada. On May 4, 1880, the Servant of God, as Superior, arrived in Palermo with a few fellow sisters to open a house of the Congregation there. In fact, during the five years she resided on the island, Sister Anna del Salvatore brought into being numerous new communities, which were soon constituted as a Province: of which the Servant of God was named Provincial Superior. These years were not without serious health troubles, accentuated by the austere, poor, and penitential life she led. In May 1885 she fell gravely ill, but out of obedience she still had to make a journey to Trapani. Having returned to Palermo, her condition grew still worse. On June 7, 1885, having received the last sacraments, comforted by the presence of her fellow sisters, she fell piously asleep in the Lord. The following week the solemn funeral rites and burial took place, while two years later her mortal remains were recognized and buried separately in a "place of deposit."

Content of the "Positio"

The Positio begins with the General Relator's Presentation: it briefly treats the origins of the Cause, the contents of the Ordinary Process and the supplementary diocesan Inquiry, the difficult Florentine situation that was so critical for the Servant of God, and finally the three monographs dedicated to her, with particular appreciation for the one written by Count Gian Ludovico Masetti Zannini.

The Informatio opens with a succinct biographical sketch of the Servant of God, followed by the course of the Cause and by the testimonial and documentary evidence. It then moves on to the presentation of the heroic exercise of virtues, first examining the virtues in general, then the theological virtues of faith, hope, and charity towards God and towards one's neighbor, particularly towards her fellow sisters and towards the sick, the poor, and the weakest; the cardinal virtues of prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance are then presented, followed by the virtues of poverty, chastity, obedience, and humility, all heroically exercised by the Servant of God. The Informatio concludes with the enumeration of supernatural gifts, with her reputation for holiness and the fama signorum, with an exposition of the salient features of her spirituality, and finally with the present-day relevance of Sister Anna del Salvatore's Christian message.

The following section consists of the Summarium of the two Palermo processes, namely the Ordinary Process, which saw the examination of 6 witnesses, all de visu, between 1896 and 1907, and the supplementary diocesan Inquiry, in which no fewer than 26 witnesses were called to testify between 1995 and 2000, most of them de auditu a videntibus. More important than the procedural Summarium, since this is a historical cause, is the Summarium documentorum. This is in practice arranged in six parts: after some brief biographical notices of certain figures of particular relevance in the course of the Positio, a collection is presented of: a. Personal documents of the Servant of God, 14 in all; b. Documents strictly relating to the critical Florentine episode, 28 documents grouped into 20 items; c. The Servant of God's correspondence, that is, an anthology of 78 of the 349 letters she wrote that have come down to us, namely 63 letters to Mother Rosa Gattorno, 11 to various fellow sisters, and 4 letters to others; d. The votes of the theological censors and the Report of the Historical Commission; e. Procedural and extra-procedural documents on the reputation for holiness, both in life and in death, of the Servant of God; and finally f. Studies on the Servant of God, represented by two biographical writings, the work respectively of Onorata Colli and of Cecilia Roberta Frati.

The last section of the Positio, bearing the title Biographia documentata, is in practice an extensive biographical monograph written by Count Gian Ludovico Masetti Zannini: it is a critical approach to the Servant of God's biographical course, in which, on the basis of the procedural and documentary data, a comprehensive and detailed reading of the Servant of God's life and activity is offered. The Positio closes with the index of names and places of the Biographia documentata alone, and a rich iconographic apparatus.

Observations on the "Positio"

1. The first observation concerns the sui generis composition of the present Positio, at least as regards the Summarium documentorum and the Biographia documentata. Normally our historical Positiones rightly give substantial weight and value to the Biographia documentata, within whose body the main documentary pieces are inserted, duly worked up and then reproduced in whole or in part in an appendix to the various chapters. It must be said, however, that in the context of our Positio this particular arrangement has its own specific importance and justification. In fact, precisely because it is a historical cause, the documentary section, or Summarium documentorum, occupies the principal place, both qualitatively and quantitatively: no fewer than 374 pages are devoted to the documents, while the Biographia documentata occupies only 220, to which must be added the other two shorter biographies, contained in 80 pages. The breadth of the Summarium documentorum partly makes up also for the shortcomings of the Ordinary Process of Palermo: this was in fact limited to the examination of only six witnesses de visu, was often interrupted for reasons of an external nature, while of a Rogatory Process certainly held before the Curia of Pontremoli, no trace exists to this day.

Rightly, the drafters of the Positio identify as the load-bearing pillars of its evidentiary apparatus, on the one hand, the testimonial evidence, as can be gathered from the Ordinary Process and the diocesan Inquiry, and on the other, the documentary evidence, acquired through historical research, whose importance has already been highlighted. These are in fact primary sources, which give a very solid foundation to the whole structure of the Positio. Besides the Servant of God's correspondence, from which her historical journey and spiritual path can be gathered directly, the personal civil and religious documents deserve special mention and appreciation, as they allow the certification of the most important stages of Sister Anna del Salvatore's biographical development. The weight of the procedural testimonies, however, is different: while the six de visu witnesses of the Ordinary Process are important, it must be said that their range of knowledge is rather limited, both chronologically and geographically, since it is largely confined to the period of the Servant of God's stay in Sicily in the last years of her life, whereas the diocesan Inquiry is particularly important for the uninterrupted continuation of Sister Anna del Salvatore's reputation for holiness down to our own day.

Special merit must be attributed to the Report of the Historical Commission, written by the late Archbishop of Monreale, Monsignor Cataldo Naro, and by Sister Anna Roberta Frati. In addition to the precise enumeration of the archives consulted and the presentation of the documentary holdings, it offers an accurate evaluation of the documentation found, directly related to the purposes of drafting the Positio: for these reasons it outlines in broad strokes the Servant of God's biographical development and, above all, clearly sketches her spiritual physiognomy, centreed on the spirit of prayer, penance, charity, and kindness, made living and fruitful by a luminous faith and a firm humility; on this same documentation is based the heroic practice of the virtues and the reputation for holiness of Sister Anna del Salvatore, clearly visible throughout the whole span of her life, in death, and after death.

One aspect on which the Positio often insists is the characterization of the Servant of God's particular spirituality: its cornerstones are the continual search for God's will, renunciation of her own plans, obedience to the Superior General in every circumstance, joyful or sorrowful. Characteristic of her spirituality are assiduous prayer, often prolonged day and night, understanding and love for her fellow sisters, a spirit of withdrawal and self-concealment, generous charity towards her brothers and sisters, above all the poorest and most suffering, following the example of Christ the Savior, whose name she bore, and in the footsteps of St. Anne, Mother of the Immaculate Virgin Mary. Both the Servant of God's rich correspondence and the procedural depositions highlight in Sister Anna del Salvatore's spiritual edifice the search for God's will and love, observance of the Rule, unconditional obedience, the spirit of prayer and penance, maternal self-giving, and charity towards the poor. This is a path faithfully walked by the Servant of God throughout her life, and one that can prove exemplary for every Christian and every consecrated person even in our own day.

As has already been said, some sections of the Positio are especially commendable: one might think, for example, of the Report of the Historical Commission, but also of the Biographia documentata: in it, besides the complete outline of the Servant of God's biographical course, the broad historical panoramas deserve a word of praise, relating for example to the historical and social setting of Marianna Orsi's birthplace, or to the superb Chapter XVII, which presents a historically and critically flawless picture of the socio-cultural and religious conditions of Sicily in the wake of the Garibaldian epic and the suppression of religious corporations, soon replaced by other pastoral initiatives such as Blessed Giacomo Cusmano's "Boccone del Povero." A good section is also the one devoted to the course of the Cause, where it is clarified, as regards the Ordinary Process, that the delays were all due to causes extrinsic to the Process itself, which was interrupted in 1907, and whose records were found, after tenacious and careful research, only in 1993.
