A word of praise is also due to the iconographic apparatus at the end of the Positio: in it are reproduced topographical plans, photographic illustrations of the house where she was born and of the buildings where the Servant of God lived, and finally images and portraits of the people with whom Sister Anna del Salvatore lived in closest contact.

6. The non-positive elements found in the Positio are entirely marginal. Among these one may note the fragmented and non-sequential pagination of the whole Positio, and consequently an incomplete index of names, limited to the Biographia documentata alone, that is, to about a fifth of the Positio. Greater care was needed in compiling the index of names: indeed, nowhere in the course of the Positio, nor in the index, can we find the first name of the Piarist Andreotti, who is always given only by his surname; the same is true of the physician Baccani, or of Mr. Baldi, or of the Archbishop of Florence Cecconi, and of numerous others; conversely, many figures, especially nuns of St. Anne, are listed in the index only by their first name, without a surname. The one real error, though this too entirely marginal, is found in note 4 on p. 500: it concerns the birth year of Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, which is not 1885 but rather 1851.

Questions of the Most Reverend General Relator

Having briefly presented the content of the Positio and made a few observations on it, we may answer with full confidence the questions formulated by the Most Reverend General Relator.

The first question concerns the completeness, sufficiency, and adequacy of the documentary research aimed at illustrating the Servant of God's life and activity: this is answered, without a shadow of doubt, affirmatively.

The second question of the Most Reverend General Relator refers to the validity and historical reliability of the documentation found and used in the Positio. The answer is likewise affirmative.

3. The final question seeks to determine whether the documentation gathered contains the elements necessary to provide a solid historical foundation for forming a judgment on the uninterrupted reputation for holiness and on the heroic exercise of virtue by the Servant of God. This third question, too, is answered affirmatively, salvo meliori iudicio.

Marianna Orsi was born in Albareto, province of Parma, on February 22, 1842, the daughter of Angelo and Domenica Mussi. Raised in a very religious environment, she received only the barest schooling and chiefly worked as a housekeeper, until she received the habit of a Daughter of St. Anne and the name Sister Anna del Salvatore in Piacenza on March 28, 1869. After having worked as a nurse in various localities of Liguria, she made her temporary profession on July 26, 1873. She then spent a brief period at San Martinello — San Martino ai Colli — in the province of Perugia; then in 1874 she was sent to Florence with the office of Superior. She remained there three years, from 1875 to 1878, trying to organize as well as possible the service the sisters gave to the suffering, until, following misunderstandings with the local clergy, she was removed and sent as Superior to Appignano, in the province of Macerata.

That same year, 1878, at the Mother House of the congregation in Piacenza, she underwent a kind of trial by her fellow sisters, accused of being responsible for the problems that had arisen in Florence; in the end she was removed from the office of Superior and sent to Ferrara in August of that same year, 1878. Shortly afterwards she was transferred to Rome to direct the "House of repentant women," then in 1879 as Superior to Sermoneta, in the province of Latina, and from there to Ovada, in the province of Alessandria.

After so much traveling from one end of Italy to the other, in 1880 she was assigned to found a house in Palermo with the office of Superior and the task of overseeing home care for the sick. Here she made her perpetual profession and, esteemed and encouraged both by the clergy and by the well-to-do classes, gave impetus, as Visitator of Sicily, to the founding of new works caring for the sick. In 1884 all the Sicilian houses became an autonomous province, and she assumed the office of Provincial, continuing her work on behalf of the elderly and the sick. She died in Palermo on June 7, 1885.

The Positio super vita, virtutibus et fama sanctitatis of this figure, who lived only forty-three years and was a nun for only sixteen, presents itself as weighty from every point of view, above all the physical one: about a thousand pages! As usual divided into many parts, fascicles and booklets, concluded by a collection of plates, gathered in twenty-three glossy pages.

The first fascicle of this voluminous anthology consists of the Presentation by the General Relator, Friar Ambrogio Eszer, O.P., and runs twelve pages. Next come the Informatio, of a hundred and twenty pages, and a page containing the text of the decree on the validity of the informative process and of the supplementary diocesan Inquiry. Then, over ten pages, the index of witnesses, both of the Ordinary Process held in Palermo in the years 1896-1907, and of the supplementary Inquiry carried out in the same city in the years 1995-2000.

The bulkiest part is the Summarium, which runs to no fewer than five hundred ninety pages; this is followed by the text of the Biographia documentata, of two hundred thirty-four pages, concluded by an indispensable index of names and places.

Unfortunately, as not infrequently happens, all these fascicles have independent pagination and require elaborate methods of cross-referencing and a jumping consultation of the various parts with the help of various kinds of bookmarks that, by their shape, signal which section of the volume one wishes to attend to or emphasize a paragraph or a document in...

Such an elaborate and multiform structure forces one to go looking, leafing through this whole hefty bundle of papers, for what one would normally find at the beginning or end of a homogeneous volume.

Indeed, the abbreviations and acronyms used in the course of the exposition are deciphered on p. 135 of the Summarium, where only four archives cited in abbreviated form are explained. The published and unpublished sources, and the bibliography used, on the other hand, are listed on pp. 9-12 of the Biographia documentata, perhaps with a slight imprecision. Indeed, on p. 9, among the unpublished sources, some works are listed that, from the notes provided — author, place and, presumably, year of printing — appear to have been printed, and in that case would more properly belong among the published sources, whose list is found on the following page. Probably, however, these are citations that, in trying to be too precise, give rise to confusion, and one does not know whether to consult those works as archival material or library books.

The presentation of the archives consulted, fourteen in all, including those in which nothing of interest was found, is found on pp. 285-286 of the Summarium, giving brief accounts of what was found in them, while it is noted, and worth noting, that most of the useful material comes from the Historical Archive of the Daughters of St. Anne. Strangely, this list does not include the Archiepiscopal Archive of Palermo, in which at least all the material relating to the two processes held in that curia must be kept, and where, as noted on p. 15 of the Informatio, in 1993 the text of the first process held in that city, interrupted in 1907, was finally rediscovered.

Moreover, this presentation of the archives consulted appears purely formal, since most of the transcribed or cited documentation is drawn from the copies inserted in the text of the Ordinary Process, always referring to its pages and only occasionally giving complete archival information on the location of the document's original.

On pp. 286-287 of the Summarium, moreover, brief mentions are given of some published writings concerning the Servant of God. The bibliography consulted, in an unusual way, is listed as many as three times in the body of the biographical account. Indeed, a first list of works, both of a general nature and those more closely concerning Orsi and the settings in which she lived, is given on pp. 10-12. A second bibliography, concerning in this case the history of the Servant of God's native village, is presented on pp. 48-50. Finally, on pp. 157-158, works concerning the history of Sicily in the nineteenth century are listed. These last two lists of printed works are placed at the end of two monographs, commissioned from expert scholars and inserted in the course of the biographical narrative.

Despite this varied structure, due to a drafting history carried out by many hands and not coordinated or finally worked up by a single supervisor, and this unusual placement of the essential information needed to grasp the research carried out, the documentation produced appears voluminous, well-organized, and dense with information, the fruit of a thorough search conducted wherever it could be presumed that documents concerning the Servant of God or her work might exist.

From this point of view, the Summarium proves to be an extremely rich anthology of first-hand documentation, of reliable testimonies, of essential writings both for reconstructing the stages of Orsi's existence and for contextualizing her work, and for entering into her ideals and her deepest motivations.

Indeed, on pp. 43-86 the essential features are given of the testimonies of six witnesses "de visu," who knew the Servant of God very closely in the last years of her life and gave their statements in Palermo between 1896 and 1907. Among them, Ignazio Zuccaro (1839-1913), from 1896 Bishop of Caltanissetta, who was very close to Orsi from her arrival in Palermo; Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi (1849-1913), who succeeded the Servant of God as Provincial of Sicily; Enrico Filiti (1846-1919), confessor of Sister Anna del Salvatore; and three other fellow Daughters of St. Anne.

On these figures and others whose names appear frequently in the documentation, brief biographical notes are given on pp. 138-142, unfortunately not supported by any bibliographic or archival reference.

There follows, in the same fascicle, on pp. 143-278, a valuable collection of documents concerning the Servant of God: civil registry documentation, documentation concerning her Florentine stay, and finally her correspondence, which gathers letters ranging from 1872-1873 to 1885. The texts are all drawn from the transcriptions inserted in the public copy of the process.

Very extensive is the collection of documentation contained between pp. 297-509, concerning her reputation for holiness in life and after death; this section contains writings of various kinds, published articles, letters, reports, writings by other authors speaking of her and her work, remembrances, and anything else containing judgments, assessments, and testimonies useful to the purpose.

The Summarium closes by reproducing the texts of two biographies of the Servant of God, one written just a few years after her death. This is the work of Onorata Colli, Cenni storici della vita di suor Anna del Salvatore Orsi, printed in Rome in 1893 in a hundred and twenty-two pages. The work, transcribed on pp. 511-569, is both a linear narrative of the Servant of God's life story and a spiritual portrait of her that, from the facts narrated, brings out her gifts and her spirituality with a delicate and thoroughly feminine touch.

There follows the edition of a much more recent and much shorter biography: Roberta Cecilia Frati, Suor Anna del Salvatore Orsi, Turin, 1995, a short popular work of only twenty-four pages, but grounded in documentation that had been gathered in those years alongside the Palermo process. It is transcribed here on pp. 569-586.

As will have been noticed, the Summarium appears to be the fruit of thorough and complete research, and what is published in it, although with some gaps or methodological uncertainties, appears as the indispensable foundation for proceeding to draft a biography of the Servant of God based on the rich documentation found.

Thanks to it, all the stages of her brief existence, marked by impulses and misunderstandings, surges of vitality and disappointments, are reconstructed in the Biographia documentata, which opens with a broad chapter devoted to the village of Albareto, where the Servant of God was born and grew up, on pp. 13-50. All the stages of her life as a nun are then narrated, including, in Chapters VII-XIV, from p. 75 to p. 118, the complicated and, for Orsi, painful affair of the founding of the Florence house, in which she found herself caught up in clerical squabbles and was at times the victim of jealousy and envy on the part of her own fellow sisters.

Her fruitful Sicilian activity is sketched with a wealth of information in Chapters XVII-XXV, on pp. 127-206, and here the Servant of God's personality and her charitable work fully emerge, well framed within the religious, economic, and social setting of Sicily in the wake of the island's annexation to the Italian dominions.

We believe, in sum, that within the complexity of the present anthology one can readily find what is useful for forming a considered judgment on Orsi's life and virtues. Indeed, the search for published and unpublished material useful to this end appears thorough and exhaustive. The list of archives consulted, despite the gaps noted, appears to indicate well-conducted research, even though most of the useful material seems to be gathered in the Historical Archive of the Daughters of St. Anne of Rome, which appears to be adequately cataloged.

Preserved here are both the letters of the Servant of God, with the shelf mark, as noted on p. 188 of the Summarium, B.6.115 and B.7.116, and the letters addressed to her, as well as the congregation's governmental acts, as well as memoirs and writings of various kinds which, if they do not directly concern her movements and activities, certainly prove useful for placing her life within the events of her congregation.

Except in the rare cases where the material was acquired after the process ended, such as some letters concerning the Florentine affair, unfortunately for all these writings detailed archival citations are very rarely given; instead one is limited to generic references, drawing directly on the copies of them inserted into the public copy of the process, so that it appears impossible to verify whether the transcriptions produced fully correspond to the originals preserved there.

More detailed are the citations of material drawn from the Archiepiscopal Archive of Florence, which, incidentally, is contained in just a few specific folders, and often also those of material drawn from the Archive of the Vatican Secretariat of State, while at other times a useless reference is made to the ASV, useless because a document cited in this way, given the vastness of that archive, seems hopelessly impossible to locate. Incomprehensible, as noted, is the absence of documentation from the Archiepiscopal Archive of Palermo. Rich in precise information are the investigations carried out in the parish archives, especially that of the Servant of God's native village, Albareto. It might perhaps have been worthwhile also to carry out some investigation in the municipal and diocesan archives of the Sicilian localities where the Daughters of St. Anne ran charitable institutions in the years of her governance: Agrigento, Acireale, Gela, etc.

All this material, consisting of writings of various kinds, has not only been extensively published but examined, framed, explained, and annotated, even though references to the sources of information are not always adequately given, while some detail of the published texts remains obscure for lack of an explanatory note.

Purely by way of example, we note that it would have been most useful to annotate the petitionary letter of December 8, 1894, transcribed on pp. 305-308 of the Summarium. Identifying the signatories would have shown its full significance; indeed it bears the signatures of the whole ruling class of Palermo, ecclesiastical and lay, including three bishops, the prior of the Dominicans, a most powerful cousin of Francesco Crispi, the former general corrector of the Minims, many urban parish priests, and a long line of nobles and titled persons who held economic and political power in the city. On many of these figures, for example Cirino, Lancia di Brolo, di Maggio, Fitalia, etc., it would not have been difficult to find biographical entries in dictionaries or even to locate monographs devoted to them.

In any case, the vast bulk of documentation acquired, transcribed in the four volumes of the public copy, here reproduced in the very extensive Summarium, has given the author of the biography all the necessary information at his disposal, often detailed down to the smallest particulars, which, properly framed, have given us a straightforward yet highly detailed profile of the Servant of God, and a varied range of judgments on her person and her work, always positive, apart from the misunderstandings mentioned above.

Therefore, since the research conducted appears exhaustive, without significant gaps, since the documentation produced appears complete and credible and not artificially selected, since it has been worked up with rigor and historical sense, we believe that in this voluminous anthology all the elements can be found for assessing the life, virtues, and reputation enjoyed by the Servant of God, and we answer affirmative to the three questions proposed.

We take the liberty of adding a brief explanatory note regarding the interruption of the Palermo Ordinary Process, begun on September 2, 1896, which proceeded with a peaceful, thoroughly Mediterranean slowness until November 19, 1907, and then was inexplicably interrupted.

To understand this interruption, which was not concluded by any formal legal act, one must keep in mind the Sicilian events of the period. Indeed, a year later, on December 28, 1908, there occurred the catastrophic earthquake of Messina, which destroyed northeastern Sicily and southern Calabria. Then all the active forces of the two regions, clerical and anticlerical alike, were heavily committed first to relief for the survivors and then to the work of reconstruction. Obviously, in those circumstances, when very concrete problems had to be addressed, especially those concerning the many orphans, there was no time to think of beatification processes.

From the documentation gathered in the section attesting to Orsi's reputation for holiness, one notes a renewed interest in her, and the process, still not concluded in 1913, a date to which many documents transcribed there go back, but then came the First World War, which delayed the economic and social recovery of the earthquake-stricken regions, and then Fascism, which completed the work of reconstruction but directed it, with evident complicity from high and low clergy, towards its own propagandistic ends, and would not tolerate interference with the exaltation of its own values, so that the good intentions attested by the documentation dating to 1927 — a moment when both the Church and the Fascist state had other concerns and were working out a strategy of peaceful coexistence — came to nothing.

The Second World War, although it ended in Sicily in 1943, made it necessary to organize further relief for the victims of bombing, more shelters for orphans and the maimed, and to plan yet another reconstruction of the destroyed institutions, including charitable, educational, and health-care ones.

Then, with the economic recovery of the 1960s, other ferments developed within the Sicilian church, and that process interrupted in 1907 was forgotten; indeed, the dossier itself was even lost, not to be found again until 1993...

1. Presentation of the Structure of the "Positio" on the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore, for the Purposes of the Judgment on the Merits

The Positio on Anna del Salvatore, in religion Maria Anna Orsi, consisting of a single volume, carries, on the page before the title page, a photograph of the Servant of God. It includes, with all the other elements required by the norms, the Informatio837 — preceded by the Presentation838 of the Relator of the Cause and General Relator of the Congregation for the Causes of Saints, Father Ambrogio Eszer — the Summarium Processi Ordinarii Panormitani;839 the Biographia documentata.840 The Positio is completed by the index841 of names and places, by the general index842 and by XXIII Plates.843 It would have been desirable for the index of names and places to extend to the whole volume rather than being limited to the Biographia documentata alone. The informational card prefixed to each testimony is commendable, giving important notices that help situate the witness in time and place and their relations with the Servant of God, both for the Ordinary Process of Palermo844 (years 1896-1907) and for the Supplementary Diocesan Inquiry of Palermo845 (years 1995-2000).

The Positio is complete with regard to documentary sources, with research extended both to archives and to primary sources, and with a corresponding bibliography; it is accompanied by a historical-scientific apparatus. It reconstructs, as a whole, in broad strokes, the socio-political situation of Italy and the particular condition of Sicily at the time.

The documentary material found confirms the conviction, already unanimously expressed by the procedural testimonies and above all by high-ranking ecclesiastical figures, of Anna del Salvatore's "holiness." In an overall look at the Servant of God's whole life, from her vocational choice to her activity as a nun, as Superior of houses and as Provincial Superior, it can be affirmed that she sanctified herself also through atrocious physical and moral sufferings, endured for long years in silence, abandonment, and solitude, without ever losing hope and openness to dialogue, in radical humility, in tenacious fidelity to the charism of the Daughters of St. Anne.

It is worth giving a brief glance at the socio-political situation of post-unification Italy. An apostolic and social action such as that of Anna del Salvatore was called for by the demands of "an age strongly shaken by the historic institutional, political and ideological transition, which placed the Church and the nascent State in a relationship of tension and clear opposition"846 or of mutual indifference, worsening the position of the working class, especially the poorest and the sick. It was a social age in which the ills could be summed up in the "cursed triangle — workshop, hovel, tavern — which was not seriously taken into consideration either by the Church or by the State,"847 but by the newly rising religious Congregations. To the social problems were added moral ills.

2. Summary of the Life of the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore. Two Important House Foundations: Florence and Palermo. Persecutions and Slanders Suffered at the Florence House

We summarize848 a brief biography of Maria Anna Orsi. She was born in Albareto, province of Parma, diocese of Pontremoli, on February 22, 1842, the daughter of Angelo and Domenica Mussi, the eldest of eight siblings, two girls and six boys. She received from her family, in her earliest years, a proper and dignified human and Christian education; her father taught her to read and write. She did not marry, owing to an inner call to consecrate herself to God. She began her novitiate in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne in Piacenza on March 28, 1869, taking the new name Anna del Salvatore. From the Foundress, Anna Rosa Gattorno, she received important assignments such as directing the Florence House and founding the Palermo House; she also lived and worked in the cities of Genoa, Milan, Macerata, Naples, Rome, San Martinello near Perugia, Sampierdarena, Sestri Ponente, Sermoneta, Ovada, and Ferrara. In every house where she lived, while reserving for herself all the humblest tasks — laundress, doorkeeper, nurse, almsgiver — she devoted hours upon hours to prayer and to adoration of the Blessed Sacrament; she had no bed of her own and was extremely strict with herself about food; she was always cheerful. Gaetano Gabriele testified: "Skilled in women's handiwork at night, always at night, she made cloth flowers to make branches to adorn the altar, or sewed the community's garments, or made lace for the chapel's use."849 As Superior, she directed the Florence House from November 20, 1875, to April 23, 1878, with fidelity and exactness to the charism of the Daughters of St. Anne to the point of heroism, but also with tenacity, constancy, deliberation, and balance, without fanaticism, intent not only on instilling a serious spirit of service in her companions but also engaging with administrative acts and with the resolutions of daily life carried out with extreme practicality, simplicity, straightforwardness, and concreteness — all qualities of a seriously human and heroically Christian woman. She was Provincial Superior of all the houses of the Sicilian Province from May 1884. She died a martyr of obedience. Sister Paolina Viani thus testifies to the last days of the Servant of God's life: "When the Superior (Sister Anna del Salvatore) found herself confined to bed, ill, with a fever of 40 degrees, as soon as she received a telegram from the Mother (the Foundress Rosa Gattorno) she got up at once and left for Trapani, and returned that evening still fasting, having taken nothing but Communion, which could have further restored her because she had taken nothing that day, and then she took to her bed never to rise again."850 The Servant of God died in Palermo on June 7, 1885. It is shown — from an overall look at the studies and testimonies in the Positio — that Anna del Salvatore practiced heroically, throughout the whole span of her existence, the cardinal and theological virtues and the evangelical counsels, following the Church's teaching and the directives of Anna Rosa Gattorno.

At this point, before taking up the charism of the Daughters of St. Anne, it is fitting to offer a brief historical reminder of woman's position in the Church. From the late Middle Ages until the French Revolution, the ecclesiastical hierarchy held to the principle that a woman's consecration to the Lord had to be strictly bound to the cloister, that is, to separation from the world and renunciation of active apostolate. "With the decree of Boniface VIII, 'Circa pastoralis,' reinforced by Pius V in 1566, women were left with only this dilemma: to preserve religious life by renouncing all apostolate, or to consecrate themselves to the apostolate by renouncing religious life."851

A) The passage of time had profoundly altered civil and religious society, and particularly enlightened figures, such as Rosa Venerini (1656-1728), had overcome such constraints. Society had undergone transformations with the French Revolution and with the political ideas of Italian unity, to the point of denying any dignity of existence to certain ecclesiastical institutions, among them monastic institutions. Some ecclesiastics of the archiepiscopal curia of Florence, such as Luigi Ciaranfi, episcopal delegate for religious life, not only failed to understand these irreversible changes but, out of ignorance or malice, also disregarded ecclesiastical norms such as the Decretum laudis of April 1876, granted to the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, by virtue of which that Institute depended on the diocesan bishop only for apostolic activities, while "its internal order and administration were reserved to the Holy See."852 The Foundress Gattorno had understood well the cause of the Florence Community's troubles, so much so that she wrote in her Memoirs, referring to December 1876, the following: "I went to one of our houses [Florence] and received from the confessor strong complaints about the Superior; certain things about the interior of the house, he knew that one could not understand how and who had told him. Suspicion fell on the sisters, but one could not think that certain other [persons] were responsible, since they loved her greatly, she being so good. There were certain little faults, but certainly not as he had said: that he ought to warn the Archbishop... He knew so much that one could never imagine where it came from. From the very first evening they showed me a young woman who wanted to become a nun, but for whom I felt a strong repugnance [...]. The very morning I was to leave, just after making my Communion, my God told me clearly that this young woman was the one putting together such ugly things and then telling them to the confessor, slandering the Superior and the girls."853

Let us now return to Ciaranfi's action. After reporting that the Foundress Gattorno had replaced the Superior, he proposed, on April 27, 1878, to the Archbishop of Florence, Eugenio Cecconi: "It is certain that this Institute gives cause for thought and for fear; nor is there any way to watch over it, because the one path there would be, namely that of the Confessor, is closed, since their Rules wish him wholly foreign to everything concerning the external conduct of the individuals and of the Institute [...]. Regarding these nuns [...], if it were possible, to take them away from here."854 The Foundress Anna Rosa Gattorno, on the situation of the Florence House, thus informed, on May 19, 1878, the protector cardinal, Alessandro Franchi: "Now very distressed by a trouble arisen here in Florence, where I had to go yesterday because of certain slanders and plain falsehoods, reported to the curia, which I can assure have nothing true in them. But first of all let me tell you frankly that the confessor is the trouble behind it all; because he would like to make a cloistered convent, and finding himself contradicted he stirs up [intrigues] of every kind, and finally, there being a Sister whose convulsions left her head a little weak and who decided she wanted to go home, he received her into his own house, and then accompanied her to the vicariate, telling the Superior that she was there, and the Superior went to fetch her, accompanying her to Piacenza; from this fact he grew bold, saying that there is not enough oversight, with a thousand added nonsenses, which I can assure were all devised by him, and that in confession he does nothing but speak ill of the Superiors to the Sisters, trying to make them lose their vocation. The worst of it is that the Vicar for Nuns believes him. Your Eminence knows well that we are in no way bound to submit to an internal direction on the part of the confessor."855 The Foundress, in a letter of May 23, 1878, to the same cardinal, added: "How grieved my soul is, and suffering the cruelest anguish, I cannot express. Under an oppression of slanders, new ones devised every day and then written to the Archbishop who is there [in Rome]."856 The slanders were directed not only against Sister Anna del Salvatore but also against the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, the Foundress Anna Rosa Gattorno not excepted, as can be seen in the already cited letter of April 23, 1878, from the episcopal delegate for religious life, Luigi Ciaranfi, to the Archbishop of Florence, Eugenio Cecconi: "This Superior and Foundress has a son who lives as a vagabond around Florence and often goes to the Institute; she also has a married daughter, and when she comes to Florence she lodges with her husband and a little daughter of hers at the Institute and stays there several days."857

The real situation of the Archbishop of Florence and some of his collaborators is well described, in summary form, in a letter from Monsignor Attilio Giovannini, parish priest of San Lorenzo in Florence, addressed to the Foundress Gattorno on June 18, 1878, in these terms: "I am not surprised that the archbishop remains firm in his judgment; unfortunately this is his habit, which has been the chief cause of his ruin in the diocese. He listens to no one but those three or four suspicious courtier-like individuals who play him to their own advantage, leaving all the responsibility with him. No one is respected here; it is enough to contradict him to be cast aside and held in suspicion by the malign influence of the few counselors who scheme in the dark and ruin everything. The prudent stay silent and only trust that the truth will make its own way, and that Rome will remedy this mess."858 Father Mauro Ricci, a Piarist, in a letter to Archbishop Cecconi of May 29, 1878, takes issue with the delegate for religious women, Ciaranfi, who cares only for his own authority, and defends the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, in these terms: "Ciaranfi cares about the authority you delegated to him, I care about yours, and about your name, which I should like to see honored as it deserves. The way certain fussy and touchy people behave does not seem to me a fitting means to that end — making an argument out of women's gossip and worthless trifles to say to a religious Institute: Kill yourself. In conclusion, this is all the demands regarding the Nuns of St. Anne amount to. Do not believe, I beg you, everything that distinguished men scheme, who however, through inexperience, are fit neither to know the world nor the monastery."859

Let us make brief mention, at this point, of an anonymous letter. We hold that anonymous slanderous writings do not deserve to be taken into consideration, let alone preserved, but ought to be destroyed at their source. The drafters of the Positio, in their commitment to documentary objectivity, saw fit to reproduce an anonymous letter860 — undated, grammatically poor, full of spelling errors, with coarse and vulgar language, a heavily dialectal vocabulary, and obscene slanders — which reveals the sordid fantasies of whoever wrote it.

The Archbishop of Florence had decided, following the above-mentioned request from Ciaranfi dated April 27, 1878, to expel861 the Daughters of St. Anne, ordering the Foundress Gattorno to dissolve the Florence House, which she, as a holy woman, had defended, through repeated efforts, with truth and justice. Gattorno implores the Archbishop, in a letter of June 7, 1878: "Ah! For pity's sake, forgive the house and punish me, tell me what I have done and I am ready to do penance for it."862 The Archbishop remained unbending in his determinations, not only confirming them but setting — in his reply to Gattorno of June 30, 1878 — October 31 as the final deadline: "The Daughters of St. Anne shall cease to be recognized as a religious Family in my diocese."863 Gattorno did not lose heart and was extraordinarily tenacious in seeing innocence triumph, going so far as to ask, in a letter of October 5, 1878, that Archbishop Cecconi "once again make trial of the due submission of myself and my Sisters to Your Excellency's authority."864 The Archbishop, in a letter of October 22, 1878, granted Gattorno's request in these terms: "Reverend Mother, I do not wish to refuse the warm and respectful entreaty which you address to me in your most esteemed letter of the 5th of this month, to make a further trial of the due submission of yourself, and of your Sisters, to ecclesiastical Authority."865

B) Sister Anna del Salvatore, by order of the Foundress, on May 4, 1880, with the office of Superior, found herself866 in Palermo to open a home-nursing house, and later, in 1883, was named Visitator of the Communities of Sicily, and in May 1884 the first Provincial Superior of Sicily. Gaetano Gabriele, in the funeral oration at the Servant of God's obsequies, after recalling the harm done to the Church and the poor by the subversive laws of Italian unity, declared: "Well then, the first to set foot in this land of sacred memories and glorious traditions was our Sister Anna del Salvatore [...]. Her virtues soon made her popular and esteemed by every class of people [...]. I will not enumerate for you all she did to advance the Institute in the service of suffering humanity. San Martino delle Scale, Termini Imerese, Sciacca, Sambuca, Aci, Sant'Antonio, Girgenti, Linguaglossa, Castiglione, Adernò, Trapani marveled at the prodigies of charity and humility together hidden in Sister Anna del Salvatore's great soul. Hospitals, asylums, orphanages, educational institutes, houses of correction and reform all witnessed the heroic exercise of her duties, her wise and prudent governance, her goodness towards all [...].

What can be said of her care for the sick? She was sought by all as an angel of consolation and peace. Oh! When the Superior comes, the sufferers would commonly say, we feel better. Before her the laments on the lips of the sick cease as if by enchantment [...]. What wonder, then, that the Mother General held her in such great and holy esteem?"867

3. Anna del Salvatore's Relations with the Foundress of her Institute: Anna Rosa Gattorno

Before recounting the relations between Blessed Rosa Gattorno and the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore, we think it useful to reproduce some biographical notes on the Foundress Gattorno, drawn from the study by Antonia Bonomi, titled Rosa Gattorno, a Universal Mother: "Rosa Gattorno, beatified on April 9, 2000, by Pope John Paul II, daughter of Francesco and Adelaide Campanella, was born in Genoa. Hers was a well-off and profoundly religious family of the local upper society [...]. In the biographies she is remembered as serene, amiable, open to piety and charity, and yet firm in character. At the age of 21, on November 5, 1852, she married her cousin Gerolamo Custo and moved to Marseille. An unforeseen financial collapse forced them to return to Genoa in straitened circumstances. Within the brief span of a few years, the firstborn, Carlotta, struck by a sudden illness, was left deaf-mute, and Gerolamo's second attempt to make his fortune abroad ended in another return, this time also in poor health. Two more children were born, Alessandro and Francesco, but on March 9, 1858, Gerolamo died, followed a few months later by the youngest child. This grief marked a radical change in her life, which she would call her 'conversion' to the total offering of herself to the Lord, to his love and to love of neighbor. Under the direction of her confessor, Don Giuseppe Firpo, she made perpetual private vows of chastity and obedience on the feast of the Immaculate Conception in 1858 [...]. Already a faithful wife and exemplary mother, without taking anything away from her children — always tenderly loved and cared for — with greater availability she learned to share the sufferings of others, devoting herself to apostolic charity: 'I dedicated myself with greater fervor to pious works and to visiting hospitals and the poor sick at home, helping them as much as I could and serving them in everything.' [...]. [In] February 1864 [...] she received the inspiration [...] for a specific Foundation of her own.

Fearing she might be forced to abandon her children, she prayed, did penance, sought counsel [...]. But feeling her duties as a mother pressing ever more insistently, she wanted the authoritative confirmation of Pius IX's own word, in the secret hope of being relieved of the call. The Pontiff, in the audience of January 3, 1866, instead ordered her to begin the foundation at once [...]. Having also overcome her relatives' resistance [...] she began in Piacenza her new religious family, which on December 8, 1866, she definitively named 'Daughters of St. Anne, mother of the Immaculate Mary.' She took the religious habit on July 26, 1867, and on April 8, 1870, made her religious profession together with 12 fellow sisters [...]. Various works of service arose for the poor and sick of every illness, for the lonely, the elderly, the abandoned, for little children and the defenseless, for adolescent and young women 'at risk' [...]. On May 4 [1900] she received the Sacrament of the sick, and two days later, on May 6, at 9 o'clock, she ended her earthly journey [...]. 'An expression of a singular design of God, in her threefold experience as wife and mother, widow, and then religious Foundress, Rosa Gattorno well honored the dignity and the 'genius of woman' in her mission at the service of humanity and the spread of the Kingdom [...]. She was moved by a deep sense of justice; as a personal principle she would never forget others' needs [...]. Meticulous, scrupulous to the point of perfectionism [...]. When she set her mind on something she also grew impatient, but she knew how to follow the promptings of a sense of timing and diplomacy in order to carry out what her creative genius suggested to her, and she knew how to take advantage of circumstances.'"868

The first meeting between the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore and the Foundress Gattorno, in all likelihood, took place869 in 1868, when Maria Anna Orsi went to Piacenza to ask to be admitted among the Daughters of St. Anne; and the meetings must have continued from November 4, 1868, the day Orsi began her postulancy, through her taking of the habit on March 28, 1869, and the beginning of her novitiate until its end.

Epistolary relations between people always reveal states of mind, daily circumstances, agreement or divergence of views, requests for help, familiarity, esteem, deference. The drafters of the present Positio report that 349 letters of the Servant of God have been found, of which 326 addressed to the Foundress; sixty-three are reproduced870 among the documents. The letters span a period of about twelve years, with an average of over 26 letters a year, revealing an extremely close relationship between the two women. Rather than commenting on the letters, we think it more meaningful to reproduce only a few passages from a handful of them, so as not to spoil the freshness, genuineness, trust, submission, love, respect, and devotion of a daughter rightly enamored of her own spiritual mother — notes never divorced from the objectivity of the facts set forth, whether concerning people, activities, buildings, projects, or the concreteness of everyday affairs, always in the light of a great prophetic and charismatic force.

A) We give preference to the letters relating to the Florence House because, amid the slanders and the instrumental opposition, they reveal the shining holiness of the Servant of God. Sister Anna del Salvatore addresses the Foundress with tender expressions: Dearest Mother, Most Beloved Mother, My dearest Mother, My dear beloved Mother, Mother and dearest Mother, Most Reverend and dearest Mother, Dearest ever-dearest mother, Most beloved Superior, My dearest and most beloved Superior, Mother all my own, My dear Mama, dear little Mama. We reproduce the first letter found, datable to Sampierdarena 1872-1873: "Dearest Mother, I write to you with this my first letter to tell you I found myself truly at a loss: poor little me, so incapable, however will I manage, though I gladly perform the obedience [...]. I beg you, dear Mother, to forgive my scrawls, I do not know if you will understand me. Be glad, dear mother, that Jesus will do everything in these 20 days... The sisters are all well, they are good, the little girls are studying, all are well except Patelani who is almost always in bed, her hands and feet are swollen, I do not know what to do for her, I thought of telling the doctor. On Saturday the sisters who go begging brought four lire; I went to Mr. Balladie's for the kitchen, but did not find him home; I will go again tomorrow... Besides, we have four sick people, I try to send someone one night and not the next. I would have so much to tell you but I fear to bother you. Sister Anna Angela teaches school and takes great care of it. Mother, I tell you that as for fasting I am now being lazy about it... that it is better to work as I did before, to go out begging; but do with me as you think best; ready and obedient to your wishes."871 Another letter, datable to Sampierdarena 1873, reports: "Dearest Mother, I have finally received your dear letter, what good fortune... Yes, dear Mother, I have understood your will... that I should learn, yes, I shall learn. Last night I began, Sister Anna Angela gives me lessons, I shall learn so as to be able to do the will of my superiors..."872 The Servant of God, under date of December 24, informs the Foundress: "Dearest Mother [...] I went to the Marchioness Rispoli, she gave me 5 lire, and then to Mrs. Severini, she gave me 5 lire and 2 flasks of wine; then she told me she would go to see some ladies who would give something; indeed, Mother, the day before yesterday she brought here a countess, and this one is quite taken with us; the Marchioness Covoni came herself and brought me a cake, which I shall send to you, dear Mother... and I beg you to accept it [...]. Dear kind Mother, I beg a great favor of you, if you think it right, and it is this: that Mrs. Severini asks to be remembered if you send the Holy Father's blessing to her and to her whole family."873 Sister Anna del Salvatore, still from Florence, under date of December 28, 1875, writes to Gattorno: "Dearest Mother [...]. I also understand that you wish my letters more often [...]. Dearest kind Mother, yesterday the Countess was here, whose name I cannot now recall, and she is quite taken with the Daughters of St. Anne, and told me she has spoken with so many ladies of the congregation and they would like a school to instruct them in religion [...] and I told her I would speak to Mother about it, and then whatever Mother says will be done [...]. Today the Princess Strozzi came, she gave me 20 lire, and then told me she has thought of giving us charge of these blind people [...] of taking on the Daughters of St. Anne because she believes them the most suited [...]. I close this letter of mine asking your forgiveness for all my faults."874 The Servant of God writes to the Foundress in a letter datable to Florence 1875-1876: "Most Beloved Mother, Here I am to give you news of all that Monsignor the Archbishop told me. He received me with such kindness... I told him everything just as you told me to say [...]. Then I told him, regarding the collection, the exact words you told me to say, and he told me that within a few days he will send the permission [...]. Receive a thousand embraces in the heart of Jesus."875 Anna del Salvatore, in a letter written from Florence on January 2, 1876, reports: "My dearest Mother, I have received your dear letter. I see that you tell me you accept the orphanage for the blind. What good fortune, how glad I am. Believe me, because much good can be done with this Princess [...]. Yesterday, Saturday, the Countess Bergal sent me 20 flasks of red wine [...]. P.S. I beg a letter from you because your letters are a great comfort to me. I do not know if you received the sweet bread with the money order, if not I will worry. Another time I shall not do so again."876 The Servant of God thus, from Florence, under date of November 26, 1876, thanks Gattorno: "My dear beloved Mother [...], Yes, my dear Mama, for as long as I live I shall keep in mind so beautiful a gift as having given me permission to come there to Piacenza to see you, for truly I could bear it no longer without seeing you... And moreover for having given me my sister. My Mother, how much kindness you show me [...]. Yesterday the Marchioness Grifoni visited us, she whose Daughter we attended, and it was a visit most pleasing to me because she brought me 100 lire for the care given to her Daughter [...]. I send you my most sincere regards along with the dear Sisters and a thousand thanks from my sister, Sister Anna Fabiana [...]. Prostrate, I ask your maternal blessing and reverently kiss your hand, while having the happy fortune to be entirely yours."877

We shall not dwell on the letters concerning878 the reproaches and instrumental accusations leveled against Sister Anna del Salvatore by Canon Ciaranfi, diocesan vicar for religious women, who, as we noted in the preceding paragraph, acted out of ignorance or malice or ambition; we may now add that he also acted with arrogance and abuse of power.

From the whole Florentine correspondence it emerges that the apostolic action of the Servant of God, always carried out with a right conscience and purity of intention, had deeply touched every social stratum of Florence at the time. The Florence House had become an important center for the whole city, one which neither Gattorno nor the entire Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne could give up for the expansion of Gattorno's own founding charism.

B) The Foundress Anna Rosa Gattorno, keeping the whole Positio in view, certainly held Sister Anna del Salvatore in great esteem, trusting her always. One can affirm with historical objectivity, considering the chronology of the disputes among certain Florentine curial figures and the presence of the Daughters of St. Anne in the city, that it was especially after the Servant of God's removal from Florence (April 23, 1878) that the harshest struggles took place between Gattorno and Archbishop Cecconi. The Florence House, also thanks to the Servant of God who — following, as we have shown above, the wise directives of the Foundress, directives aimed at preserving the original charism and the House's autonomy from outside interference, the confessor not excepted — had become an important reality for the Congregation, above all for its extensive apostolic activity for the good of society. Had the charism crumbled in the important Florence House, such a collapse could have occurred elsewhere too. The distressing Florence situation had become the chief topic among the Daughters of St. Anne. In early August 1878, Sister Anna del Salvatore received879 the formal order to go to Piacenza, where the Institute's Superiors were gathered for the spiritual exercises. The Servant of God no longer dwelt on the Florence events, but was astonished at the order, because in her whole religious life the possibility of disobeying had never even crossed her mind. She expressed her astonishment to the Foundress, from Appignano, in early August 1878, in these terms: "Dear beloved Mother, Ah! What grief has just come to me, and all unexpected. How could it ever be that I should not wish to obey, when I am so glad to be able to see you? And how could I go on living if even for a single moment a single thought [of disobeying] had come to my mind? My God! After so much joy felt when I had the news that I would come to make the holy Exercises, I must feel this sharp grief that dear Mother must compel me by obedience [...], you alone can do with me as you wish, I am and always shall be yours, and I am glad to do your will and not my own; if I must come even sooner I shall be the gladder. For now I say no more, because soon I shall be in your arms and so you can do with me as you wish."880 The Superiors, during the spiritual exercises, met to find a solution that might satisfy the Archbishop of Florence and his less than exemplary collaborators. The members of the assembly of Superiors of the Daughters of St. Anne split, as usually happens in such cases, into two opposing views. Some of the Superiors thought that, by removing Sister Anna del Salvatore from the Institute, full satisfaction could be given to the Archbishop of Florence. Another group of them went881 to Gattorno to plead the rightness of the positions taken by Sister Anna del Salvatore, who had done nothing but carry out, as already shown, the Foundress's orders in the tangled Florence situation. Gattorno — a woman of governance, just, prudent, far-sighted, charismatic — managed,882 at the same time, to save her original charism, the Florence House, and the Servant of God's good name. Gattorno's relations with Sister Anna del Salvatore, even after the latter's death, are succinctly set out in the Biographia documentata, written by the Positio's collaborator, the historian Gian Ludovico Masetti Zannini, in the chapter titled "Defuncta adhuc loquitur." We reproduce only a few passages. Masetti Zannini writes thus: "The death of the Servant of God was felt by the Foundress with particular sorrow, and regarded as a trial that the Lord had given the Institute, depriving it on earth of an angelic creature. At the same time, and for a long while still, God made the Foundress's soul and the whole community feel the Servant of God's very special protection and presence, even through her own words."883 Gattorno, in August 1885, a few months after the Servant of God's death, noted in her Memoirs: "So many prophecies are made and written to me, but only one so far I see coming true, because when Sister Anna del Salvatore was alive, how many I experienced, and all true."884 Gattorno sensed in her own body, though not yet informed, the moment of the Servant of God's death (June 7, 1885), as she left written in her diary: "O blessed soul, why did you fly so soon to heaven and leave me in a sea of suffering? You were my comfort [...]. My dear Sister Anna del Salvatore; those long evenings we spent together, always speaking of things of our sweet Love. Patience! May the will of my whole Good be done."885 Sister Celsa Anna Speranza, in Gattorno's canonization process, was thus reassured by the Foundress regarding the future of the Daughters of St. Anne, a few days before her death (May 6, 1900), in April 1900: "Be at peace then, I repeat to you, for all will go well [...], at the gates stands my own Salvatore, who will protect you."886 Gattorno was present887 on February 14, 1887, at the first recognition of the Servant of God's mortal remains, and, on September 2, 1896, at the opening of the beatification process, which she herself had requested.

4. Judgment on the Merits and Historical Judgment on the "Positio" of Anna del Salvatore

The drafters of the Servant of God's Positio, but above all the documents themselves, demonstrate both the unlawful interference of ecclesiastical Authorities and the extortionate maneuvers of the Servant of God's adversaries, or rather her enemies. Encountering men such as those cited above, especially when clothed in religious authority, may represent, from a human point of view, life's misfortune, but, for the person of faith, an occasion to exercise the human and theological virtues, as it was for Anna del Salvatore.

The Positio is rich in documents that help reconstruct Anna del Salvatore's personality and human and spiritual journey. It proves unadorned, straightforward, clear: everything leads, naturally and without forcing, to the historical experts' conclusions, which recognize the Servant of God's holiness.

The drafters' honesty shows in the precision of their interpretation of the documents. The documented biography — preceded by lists of the archives consulted, abbreviations, manuscript sources, printed sources, the bibliography on the Servant of God, and the general bibliography — with archival or primary-source footnotes and the corresponding documents at the end of each chapter, offers the possibility of scientific verification.

The beatification of Anna del Salvatore, this extraordinary woman, able to fuse an intense interior life with an active love of neighbor, and whose supreme rule was always the unconditional carrying out of the divine will, would have great resonance, above all among the Daughters of St. Anne and in the places where they carry out their apostolate.

Answers to the Questions

I have examined the Positio super vita, virtutibus et fama sanctitatis concerning the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore.

I turn to the first question: I. An pervestigationes documentorum ad illustrandam vitam et operositatem Famulae Dei Annae a Salvatore rite ac plene peractae sint?

The Positio on Anna del Salvatore reflects a sound and correct historical approach.

I conclude, answering: Affirmative, to the first question, because the research can be regarded as objective and sufficient for the cause.

I turn to the second question: II. An documenta collecta et in positionem inserta fidem historicam mereantur?

Having laid that first fundamental groundwork, I express my view on the authenticity of the documents studied and published in the Positio, documents which I consider authentic and free of interpolation, since I detect no alteration from an archival or historical point of view. The documents gathered are original instruments, and are presently kept in the archive of the Mother House in Piacenza. As for the other documents coming from other archives (diocesan, parish, state, and other public bodies), there exist copies authenticated by the competent authority. The archival and biographical sources meet the required characteristics and therefore merit historical credence as regards the reconstruction of the Servant of God's life and activity. The documents found fully convey the personality, spirituality, and work of Anna del Salvatore, who emerges as a woman rich in interior life, of strong faith, sensitive to God's voice and ready to grasp and carry out his will, attentive to her neighbor's problems, ready to meet the urgent needs of the poorest, especially the abandoned sick.

I conclude, answering: Affirmative, to the second question, because the documents reproduced in the Positio deserve, as a whole and in their essentials, historical credence.

I turn to the third question: III. An in eisdem documentis ea inveniantur elementa quae solidum fundamentum historicum afferant ad iudicium de fama sanctitatis Famulae Dei atque virtutum exercitio ferendum?

It is necessary to establish, from a historical point of view, whether the Servant of God's reputation for holiness is sufficiently clear and constant, grounded in the exercise of the virtues and not artificially induced. The Ordinary Process was begun888 before the Archiepiscopal Curia of Palermo on September 2, 1896, about 11 years after the Servant of God's death.

I can affirm that the documentation of the Positio provides sufficient elements regarding the proofs of the heroic exercise of the virtues practiced by the Servant of God and of her reputation for holiness. It does not seem to me that the historian ought to enter into a detailed assessment of the heroic exercise of the theological, moral, and related virtues, but rather to assess as a whole the life of the Servant of God, which was spent living out the faith for her neighbor's good. The documentation of the Positio, carefully examined, shows, in the convergence of all the sources, that Maria Anna Orsi attained such maturity in Christian life that she can be held up by the Church as a model of a daughter, of a Christian in the service of the sick, of a woman obedient to the directives of the Church, to the charism of the Institute, and to the Foundress Anna Rosa Gattorno.

The many proofs, both in life and in death, and through the various decades since her death down to the present, show that the figure of Anna del Salvatore has always been surrounded by esteem and a reputation for holiness, cultivated above all by Gattorno, without anything ever having been said, written, or done against that reputation.

I conclude, answering: Affirmative, to the third question, because in the Positio, considered as a whole and in its essentials, are found the elements that provide a solid historical foundation for the judgment on the reputation for holiness and on the heroic exercise of the virtues of the Servant of God Anna del Salvatore.

Before examining and judging the Positio super vita, virtutibus et fama sanctitatis of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore, in religion Marianna Orsi, a professed nun of the congregation of the Sisters Daughters of St. Anne, it is well to offer a brief historical framing of this figure and above all of her role within the Church and within civil society itself.

1 — Biographical Profile

The Servant of God was born to Angelo and Domenica Mussi, in Albareto Marignano (Parma), on February 22, 1842: the eldest of nine siblings, three girls and six boys.889 At baptism, administered in the parish church, she was given the name Marianna Veronica. According to an old custom, at the age of four she received Confirmation from Monsignor Orlandi, Bishop of Pontremoli, who had gone to Albareto on a pastoral visit.890

Marianna's family owned a house at "Le Moie," a hamlet a kilometer from Albareto, a border village and crossing point divided among three dioceses, which is why many families, to better their lot, sold their property and migrated elsewhere.891 The village lacked schools, or rather, instruction "for boys" had, since 1833, been entrusted to the parish priests, a task they still held in 1870; while at the time a single school for boys and girls had not yet been considered, given the resistance of the population.892 As a result, girls were excluded, and very few parents troubled to have their daughters educated. In the Orsi family, however, Marianna was taught to read, write, and do sums, while two of the sons were sent to study at the Seminary of Bedonia.893

According to the testimony of Don Tommaso Grilli, parish priest of Albareto, the Servant of God "was a young woman of gentle character, calm in spirit, without vanity in her dress or her conduct, sincere, cheerful, yet modest in conversing with her companions, obedient, respectful. With praiseworthy patience she bore the lack of things she often needed. Being the eldest, she helped her own mother with all care and patience in raising and looking after her little brothers and sisters. In this she was certainly always greatly helped and aided by the exercise of her charity."894

It was probably as a result of the financial difficulties the family found itself in that the Servant of God, at thirteen years of age, was sent into service with two priest uncles, Don Antonio Mussi, parish priest of Buzzò, and Don Luigi Mussi, parish priest of Rovinaglia and later of Valmazzola, "going now to one, now to the other, to lend her work of good household management; but, although she got on well with her uncles, by whom she was held in the regard she deserved, she could not grow accustomed to being apart from her mother and her family, and decided to return to Albareto."895

Three years later, in 1858, she went to Bedonia to look after her two brothers Giovanni and Luigi, who attended the seminary as day students. The seminary had been entrusted to the Priests of the Mission, but they were expelled on August 30, 1850.896 The Servant of God remained there until 1862, then returned to her parents at Albareto. When they, having "incurred some debts, and in order to pay them off and in hopes of greater advantages, sold all their property," moved to Centovera (Piacenza), the Servant of God did not follow them, but stayed in the village, entering the service of her uncle Lorenzo Mussi, the local mayor.897

There the Servant of God began to feel a lively affection for the young Angelo Zecca; but, in 1866, she left the village to rejoin her family, who were at Centovera, moving later to Tuna, "near Piacenza, from where the said young woman went to the convent and took the name Sister Anna del Salvatore."898

The purpose of the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne — lay nuns founded by Rosa Gattorno (1831-1900) — which today numbers about three thousand religious, is "a special devotion to the glorious St. Anne," "home care for the sick," and the care and prevention of "girls at risk."899

The Servant of God began her novitiate in 1869. Her first field of apostolate was Liguria, the native land of the Institute's foundress, where, still a novice, she was sent to work as a nurse in various houses, and even then her fellow sisters "admired in her great humility, obedience, charity towards all, scrupulous exactness in fulfilling her duties and in observing the Holy Rule: in short, she was a great example."900 In 1873, having made her temporary profession, she was called to the office of Superior at the orphanage of Sampierdarena. The following year she moved, perhaps for health reasons, to Sestri Ponente. In 1874 she was in Perugia to start a house at San Martinello. But by the end of the following year she was already in Florence, with the charge of Superior of the "home nursing" Community. She would make solemn profession in 1881, while the Institute's rule would only be approved, ad experimentum, in 1885, the very year of the Servant of God's death.901

The scant news of her stay in Liguria — between Sampierdarena and Sestri Ponente — reaches us through the Servant of God's correspondence with the Mother Foundress.902 In 1875 the Servant of God is in Florence, where, caring for the sick at home, she also looks after a canon, recommended by Archbishop Giovannini, who "wants care day and night"; being poor, she asks the Mother for "some money, to buy things for the sick man," even though "the first gentlemen of Florence" come to visit him.903 Her affability wins the sympathy of the cardinal archbishop and of noble Florentine ladies. The workload grows, and the Servant of God asks the Mother to send her "one or two nurses"; her sister, Sister Anna Fabiana, thus joins her; meanwhile she grows fond of two girls from Fossi who ask, "even on their knees," to be sent "to the night watch" to care for the sick. She writes to the Mother that "one is 18 and the other 21" and that, even though they have not had "the happy fortune of becoming Daughters of St. Anne," they nevertheless ask permission to be able also to give "a little relief to poor humanity," and so the Servant of God intercedes for them, "so, if she permits, I will send them now and then."904 Meanwhile the Servant of God's observance of the Institute's rule becomes so scrupulous that she even asks the Foundress's forgiveness for having telephoned her dying brother, who had asked to be able to see "Sister Anna del Salvatore."905

Charitable activity is in full swing, given the requests for care, especially from the wealthy families of Florence. In three months thirty sick people had been cared for: "the Florentines vie with each other to have the Daughters of St. Anne at their bedside."906 For daily expenses the sisters go begging door to door, collecting money and goods; but there are infiltrators, against whom one must be on guard.907 Some promise generous offerings to settle the House's debts, but these do not arrive; and yet the Servant of God remains calm because "Jesus will provide, for he is my treasurer, so I think of nothing." It is in the midst of this activity that the doctor asks to examine the Servant of God's chest, fearing she may have consumption; but she writes to the Mother: "it isn't true, because I just laugh about it." This was March 1877; by May her health improves: "I am better."908

The Servant of God, as Superior, continues to receive postulants in Florence; but something is not right. The Foundress, to whom letters have come from the Curia — but also anonymous letters — tells her so, and the Servant of God accuses herself, writing that she felt great sorrow "on hearing that in that community there is so much disorder on my part," and asked that, if indeed "this happens through my fault, you, so good, may remove me so as not to give this scandal," thus placing her office in the hands of the Foundress.

From the letter, written from Florence on July 9, 1877, we learn that the sisters of the Florentine community numbered about fifteen in all: one had psychological problems, and those who accused her of not taking part in the common exercises were lying.909 There was also the problem of priests circling around the house, giving rise to misunderstandings with the episcopal Vicar for religious life in the diocese of Florence. Since April 1876 the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne had obtained the Decretum laudis, and was thus exempt from ordinary jurisdiction, except as regards simple apostolic activity. Neither the confessor nor the episcopal delegate for religious life had understood this. The confessor Niccolai, having had a Jansenist-style formation on the Eucharist, could not even conceive of the norms that, on this matter, would be laid down twenty-five years later by St. Pius X, and so had taken great offense that he had not been asked for authorization to allow some little girls, who had made their First Communion only a day before, to make a second communion; he had thus slammed the door, saying he no longer wished to come to hear confessions.910 Canon Ciaranfi, episcopal vicar for the nuns, had for his part distorted the Servant of God's words, attributing to her the decision to remove Father Andreotti, who had offered to give the sisters lessons free of charge; until a strict order came from Rome forbidding Andreotti to go to the community.911 The bishop, poorly informed, thinking he was faced with problems of insubordination, decided at first to close the house; but soon thought better of it.912

There were also problems of care and of household governance. Florence is large, so "several Florentine gentlemen have joined together to set up another house of the Daughters of St. Anne outside the Porta alla Croce"; while the Countess Montauti came asking for services "for her sick maid and for a sister-in-law of her own household."913 The sisters too fall ill, and, according to a severe rebuke from the attending physician, the Servant of God is said to have sent off "Sister Anna Giuseppina with bronchitis, fever, and chest pain, a patient who absolutely could not be moved," the responsibility "for this sister's health" falling on her.914

In January 1878, the Servant of God went to the Marches, on behalf of the Foundress, for an inspection of the recently opened Appignano House.915 Meanwhile, in the Florence house the situation grows worse. Given the difficulties mentioned above, the Servant of God pours out her heart to the Foundress, writing to her: "how must I conduct myself with these Florentines!", yet at the same time tells the Mother she is "ready to stay here where I am for my whole life"; while assuring her that "the schools are now going well; the little girls have been coming in great numbers for the past few days... We also have many sick people. The sisters are all well."916

The Foundress decides to transfer the Servant of God, as Superior, to Appignano (April 23, 1878).917 Arriving at Osimo late in the day, she asks the bishop for lodging, which he grants, but fears she has gone against the Mother's wishes, who had told her, "if you can, do not go to the bishop, and go straight on"; so she writes asking forgiveness for her "weakness."918 At Appignano — insecure and needing confirmation for her conduct — she turns to the local parish priest, regarding him as "the nearest superior"; but then repents and writes to the Foundress asking forgiveness: "you alone can do with me as you wish, I am and always shall be yours and am glad to do your will and not my own." She then adds: "if I must come even sooner I shall be the gladder," thus declaring her readiness to shorten her stay.919 In early August of that same year, 1878, the Servant of God receives the order to go make the spiritual exercises in Piacenza, where in mid-July the gathering of the councilors had taken place. The Servant of God was held responsible for the situation that had arisen in Florence, so that some were of the opinion that Sister Anna del Salvatore should be dismissed from the Institute; but others took up her defense. The fact is that the Servant of God is relieved of the office of Superior and assigned to the Ferrara community, where, however, she stays only briefly, since already in November 1878 she is sent to Rome to direct the "House for repentant women." Then, in January of the following year, she is sent to direct the Sermoneta House (Latina), from which, by mid-year, she moves to Ovada with the task of nurse.920 There, however, the Servant of God notices a distressing situation that the sisters keeping night watch over a certain woman had fallen into, since "they were being harassed by that madwoman's husband," and so she warns the Foundress, begging her "not to tell the Superior that I wrote to you."921

Leaving Lazio with a few fellow sisters, on May 4, 1880, the Servant of God, "after a most painful journey," is already in Palermo to open a house of "home nurses," and the Servant of God holds the office of Superior. Her welcome is good; she promptly seeks to make contact with the ecclesiastical authorities, but cannot meet the archbishop, since he is away;922 she will however go to see him on the 7th, that is, three days later.923

Of particular interest, for the exercise of the virtue of poverty, is her request to the Foundress to buy a wristwatch or a clock, without which "I do not know how to manage with the schedule."924 Reminiscent of a page from the Fioretti is the sensitivity shown by the Servant of God, who confesses and asks the Foundress's forgiveness for having considered it a "grave fault" that, on the occasion of the clothing of six Boccone del Povero girls, "I and the sisters went to greet them, and as they were coming out from dinner they asked me to let them have coffee, and I agreed, so that I and the sisters had coffee, then they brought us fruit, sweets, and other little things"; asking therefore for "forgiveness and penance, resolved never again to commit such faults."925 And, mark well, this was no passing scruple of conscience: so much so that, not even two months later, she again, for the same reasons, asks the Foundress's forgiveness.926 This is genuine sensitivity born of a deep sense of humility, which drives her to avoid any occasion that might distract her from a withdrawn life wholly devoted to the service of her brothers and sisters. Witness the example of permission to be a baptismal godmother, which she initially refused, but which was then "wrung from her" by relatives who, wanting the Servant of God as godmother, turned, together with Father Cusmano, to the Foundress.927

Meanwhile, in Sicily five houses had been opened. The following year the Servant of God makes her perpetual vows (July 26, 1881?)928 and, given the growing demand to open new houses, moves from place to place to conduct the respective negotiations.929 She also discharges, with wisdom, prudence, and charity, the office of Visitator of the houses, which within three years grow from five to twenty, so that in May 1884 the Communities of Sicily are constituted a Province and Sister Anna del Salvatore is named Provincial Superior. These are the last months of the Servant of God's life, during which she plays a singular role as inspector,930 mediator,931 and prophetess.932

In April 1885 the Servant of God falls gravely ill; nonetheless she goes to visit the various communities of Trapani. She dies on June 7, 1885, having received all the sacraments, surrounded by her fellow sisters, to whom she commends observance of the rule. On the following 15th, solemn funeral rites and burial in the cemetery of St. Ursula in Palermo.

2 — Content of the "Positio"

This is a cause resumed, by the historical route, about a century after the first process, instituted ten years after the Servant of God's death. The Positio, drafted at various times, consists of a single volume, arranged in two parts:

— the Informatio (pp. 1-118) with the description of the history of the Servant of God's beatification cause, from its opening to the new resumption of the Cause (5-10). It then moves on to the practice of the individual heroic virtues — heroism of the virtues in general and in particular; evangelical counsels and humility; supernatural gifts (19-92), with an account of the reputation for holiness the Servant of God enjoyed (93-110); the salient features of her spirituality and the relevance of her message today (111-118). The Decretum super validitate follows.

After this comes the Summarium, preceded by the

— Tabella-Index testium et summarii (I-IX)

— Summarium testium, in turn preceded by the interrogatories and by the articles of testimonial proof (1-41), after which the depositions of the witnesses from the first Palermo ordinary process (1896-1907) are reproduced, and from the supplementary diocesan inquiry of Palermo (1995-2000), another 26 witnesses (Summarium virtutum).

There follows the Summarium documentorum, with 15 personal documents of the Servant of God (138-156), preceded by a paragraph titled Brief Biographical Notices of Certain Figures (138-142); and 20 documents on the Florence "affair" (158-187). After this comes the Servant of God's correspondence, where 78 of the 349 letters of the Servant of God found so far are reproduced (189-278).

Still within the same section follow the votes of the theological censors and the report of the experts "in re historica" (279-296). After this come various documents on the Servant of God's reputation for holiness, divided into two sections: sixty procedural documents in all (298-431); followed by, as extra-procedural documents: accounts of graces received through the Servant of God's intercession, writings of the Foundress, excerpts of letters (432-509). Two studies on the Servant of God close the section (510-588).

The third part consists of the Biographia documentata, which, in twenty-eight chapters, traces the stages of the Servant of God's — in any case brief — life (1-220). The index of personal and place names closes the section (221-231). Outside the text, 23 Plates illustrating the territory, the places of memory, the Servant of God, and the figures with whom she came into contact or who wrote her biography.

3 — The Cause

On December 8, 1894, bearing the signatures of sixty religious and civil figures, a petitionary letter was sent to Cardinal Celesia, Archbishop of Palermo, for the opening of the Servant of God's Cause, whom "merciful God, who had granted so many favors in life... continues even after death to glorify, granting immense graces through her intercession."933 Thus, sixteen years after her death, on May 6, 1896, the ordinary informative process for the cause of beatification and canonization begins. But the organizational machinery is slow to get going, and the process undergoes various interruptions, some due to failures to observe requirements governing the course of the process.

During the Ordinary Process, 24 sessions in all were held. Only six witnesses de visu were examined, though all qualified: a bishop, two diocesan priests, and 3 nuns of the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne. Hence the supplementary diocesan inquiry, held in the years 1995-2000, more than a hundred years after the Servant of God's death, with the examination of 26 witnesses, of whom 2 ex officio, few de auditu a videntibus, with scant knowledge of the facts; the rest de auditu ab auditu.

4 — Observations on the "Positio"

In the first draft of the Informatio there were missing — something, moreover, already noted by the General Relator Father Ambrogio Eszer — the biographies, the sources (archives and libraries), and the bibliography. An attempt was made to remedy this gap with the Biographia documentata, expressly requested by the Congregation for the Causes of Saints, which the Postulation entrusted to Professor Gian Lodovico Masetti Zannini, and which was inserted at the end of the Positio as an integral part (1-234).
