In it some of the gaps left are filled, beginning with the Servant of God's novitiate, which lasted three years, her move to Sampierdarena, etc.

The documentary evidence consists of the witnesses' depositions, enriched by the Tabella-Index Testium et summarii, from which an extraordinarily strong reputation for holiness emerges, and above all by the correspondence.

The depositions of the six witnesses examined in the first process carry considerable evidentiary value, as they are able to testify on all the questions, and their depositions agree on the heroic nature of the Servant of God's virtues.934 Apparently weaker is the contribution of the 26 witnesses from the supplementary diocesan inquiry: indeed, though poorly informed about the Servant of God's life, all of them nonetheless agree on her reputation for holiness, and a good proportion attest to the heroic nature of her charity towards her neighbor and of her humility.935

While the best window onto the Servant of God's personality remains, without doubt, her correspondence, for whose assessment some notes must first be made.936 Having been taught to read and write by her parents, her sentence construction leaves something to be desired; nonetheless the Servant of God expresses herself with sufficient clarity. As for her handwriting, finally, she herself confesses to having an uncertain hand, going so far as to call it "scrawls."937 It would therefore have been fitting to include in the appendix titled "Plates" a facsimile of one of her letters as well. I note that the transcription does not always seem faithful. I observe, for example, that the same episode is placed now in Via Faenza, now in Via Foligno: I think there must have been — in one case or the other — a misreading.938 I further wonder whether the publication of the 78 autograph letters of the Servant of God, selected from the 349 found so far, was an entirely correct operation, and whether it might not have been more fitting to provide at least a calendar summary of the whole correspondence which, for reasons of space, could not be published.

From the biography and the archival documents there emerges a life wholly devoted to the service of others. As Witness I, well informed of the facts, had occasion to testify, "the Servant of God had great zeal for souls, nor did she spare herself hardship and suffering so long as she managed to do good to souls [...] ready to keep night watch to care for the sick, and also to spare the sisters."939 Documenting her activity is, as mentioned above, her correspondence with the Mother Foundress. From it emerges a woman zealous in guiding the community entrusted to her, affable with both the powerful and the humble, able to strike up dialogue at once with religious and civil authorities as well as with so-called "people who count" — dialogue made all the more indispensable by the charitable activity carried out by the Institute. There are, however, in the Servant of God's life some attitudes of insecurity that seem to cloud her figure. Her insecure, irresolute character, as it emerges from many letters, poses a problem. One wonders whether this was perhaps genuine humility, or a limited aptitude for guiding a community of religious. Looked at closely, even in the most difficult situations the Servant of God does not lose control, showing full resignation to God's will and a high degree of charity and humility, treating those around her not as their Superior but as an elder sister.

Less problematic, by contrast, is the Servant of God's conflict with Canon Luigi Ciaranfi, episcopal Vicar for religious women in Florence; nor the mooted possibility of expelling the Servant of God from the Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne. Although the Institute had obtained the Decretum laudis (April 1876), Ciaranfi acted as if the house of the nuns of St. Anne were still a simple association under diocesan law, so that in a decree of August 31, 1877, he writes: "in the governance and direction of the nuns of St. Anne no mission may be admitted that is not recognized and consented to by the diocesan ordinary."940 Ciaranfi himself, moreover, in order to accuse the Servant of God and her nuns, relies on hearsay. He informs the archbishop that "Monsignor Giovannini, prior of San Lorenzo [...], speaking to me of the said nuns of St. Anne, who are in his parish," showed himself "little satisfied with them, and especially with the local Superior, false and lying."941 And in another letter he writes that he has learned "from Father Giovanni of San [Lorenzo], Florence, that, two nuns having gone to keep night watch over a sick penitent of his, they did not conduct themselves with the reserve, or rather modesty, required not only of religious but also of Christian women."942 And he then passes a scathing judgment on the postulants: "passing along Via Faenza I saw a postulant at the window of the house, and she seemed to me a rather vain young woman: I saw the Superior for a moment, and she told me this young woman was passing through on her way to be sent to the Novitiate in Piacenza."943 And he concludes thus: "following the death of Cardinal Berardi, perhaps these nuns will have some other Most Eminent Protector; let us hope their setup turns out better, that their rules prove satisfactory, and that confessors may have some influence over the good order and morality of the house."944 Hence the transfer of the Servant of God and the closing of the House ordered by the archbishop, poorly informed of the facts.945 In reality, behind this operation lies Ciaranfi's real difficulty in influencing the house's internal life, having to work through the confessor, who, however, by their rules was "meant to be wholly foreign to everything concerning the external conduct of the individuals and of the Institute."946 And, as the Foundress Rosa Gattorno had occasion to write to Cardinal Franchi, protector of the Institute, the whole Florence affair rested on "slanders and perfectly groundless falsehoods, carried to the curia, which I can assure have nothing true in them," as she herself had been able to verify, going there in person and staying six days; while "the Vicar for Nuns believes him."947 Perhaps because, as Father Ricci of the Pious Schools had occasion to write to the Archbishop of Florence, "Ciaranfi cares about the authority you have delegated to him," while calling the accusations against the Daughters of St. Anne "women's gossip" and "insignificant trifles"; which is why he warned the archbishop, telling him: "I am sorry to see the weight of others' rashness fall upon you."948 As for the rest: the letters of Monsignor Giovannini, of Cardinal Franchi, of the Foundress; the archbishop of Florence's initial resistance to suspending the order withdrawing the nuns, and finally his acceptance of the Foundress's humble entreaty, by which he grants the nuns of St. Anne a further period of "trial," all fit within the framework of the real difficulties new institutes encounter,949 until Providence, which governs all things, dispels every obstacle set against the vindication of what is true and just — obstacles arising now from misunderstanding, now from bad faith, now from denunciation, as in the case of the young woman "who wanted to become a nun," the same one who "put together such ugly things (regarding the Daughters of St. Anne of Florence) and then told them to the confessor, slandering the Superior and the girls."950 It is not improbable that this same young woman was the author of the anonymous letter aimed at besmirching the Servant of God, who had probably dissuaded her from undertaking religious life.951

Nothing of these groundless accusations emerges from the de auditu and de visu testimonies; see Witness II, who, well informed of the facts, testifies that the Servant of God "met with contradictions and defamatory slanders; but that these were later exposed as false."952

5 — Questions of the Most Reverend General Relator

Having presented in broad outline the content of the Positio and having expressed some observations on it, I answer the questions put by the Most Reverend Postulator General.

1. The first question concerns the completeness, sufficiency, and adequacy of the documentary research aimed at illustrating the life and activity of the Servant of God: that is, whether all the existing documentation on the Servant of God's life has been examined. As already mentioned, an attempt has been made to remedy the gaps inherent in the first draft of the Positio with the Biographia documentata; so that, with the additions made in this latter section, the collection of documentation can be considered, if not complete, at least sufficient for the theological consultors to render a judgment on the merits, even though the selection of correspondence has left out all too many letters, which it would have been fitting at least to catalogue in summary form, in order to know the frequency and content of her dealings, as local Superior, with the Mother Foundress, and, in detail, the exercise of the individual virtues. It remains, in this sense, strongly indicative that the Congregation, after the presentation of the Positio, requested and obtained supplementary documentation. That said, to the first question I answer, affirmative.

2. The second question of the Most Reverend General Relator refers to the authenticity, validity, and historical reliability of the documentation found and used in the Positio. The fidelity to the Servant of God's handwriting — though a cross-check by several hands would have been useful — and to her sentence construction, she having only an elementary education, together with the sincerity with which the work was carried out, mean that the answer to the second question is of an affirmative character.

3. The third question seeks to know whether the documentation gathered contains the necessary elements to provide a solid historical foundation for formulating a judgment on the reputation for holiness and on the exercise of the virtues by the Servant of God. I consider the documentation produced in the Positio more than sufficient to reconstruct the service of charity and the spiritual journey of this Servant of God, who proves exemplary, and so to the third question as well I answer affirmative.

In summary, I answer the first, second, and third questions, affirmative, salvo semper meliori iudicio, wishing a happy outcome for the cause, this being a model of holiness of the most pressing relevance today, especially for all those who have chosen to serve the Church in Orders and religious Congregations of active life.

At the end of the reading of the Vota, no significant problems emerged.
